A skew approach to enrichment for Gray-categories Thanks: The first-named author acknowledges the support of the Grant agency of the Czech Republic under the grant 22-02964S
John Bourke, Gabriele Lobbia

Abstract
. It is well known that the category of Gray-categories does not admit a monoidal biclosed structure that models weak higher-dimensional transformations. In this paper, the first of a series on the topic, we describe several skew monoidal closed structures on the category of Gray-categories, one of which captures higher lax transformations, and another which models higher pseudo-transformations.



1.
Introduction

The idea of approaching higher-dimensional categories via iterated enrichment is an appealingly simple one. Indeed, if
\mathcal{V}
is a symmetric monoidal category, then so is the category
\mathcal{V}
-
\mathbf{Cat}
of small
\mathcal{V}
-enriched categories. Now taking
0
-
\mathbf{Cat}=\mathbf{Set}
to be the cartesian closed category of sets and defining
(n+1)\textnormal{-}\mathbf{Cat}:=(n\textnormal{-}\mathbf{Cat})\textnormal{-}\mathbf{Cat}
yields
1
-categories,
2
-categories and onwards to
n
-categories for all finite
n
. Moreover, the categories
n
-
\mathbf{Cat}
are very well behaved — in addition to be cartesian closed, they are locally finitely presentable.

The downside is that the
n
-categories obtained via this process are the strict ones. In fact, whilst every weak
2
-category, or bicategory, is equivalent to a strict
2
-category, not every weak
3
-category is equivalent to a strict one. In particular, beyond dimension
2
, strict
n
-categories are insufficiently general. This rules out iterative enrichment in
cartesian closed categories
as a framework for (weak) higher-dimensional categories.

There is an elegant solution to this problem in dimension
2
, which allows us to move one step further. Whilst
\mathbf{2}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is cartesian closed, it also admits a number of non-cartesian monoidal biclosed structures, including the lax and pseudo variants of the Gray-tensor product. The latter of these is symmetric monoidal closed, and we will refer to as the Gray-tensor product
\otimes_{p}
. It has a number of good properties.

(1)

Given 2-categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
the morphisms of the internal hom
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
are
pseudonatural transformations
, the most important transformations in 2-category theory.

(2)

The Gray tensor product equips the model category
\mathbf{2}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
with the structure of a
monoidal model category

[
29
]
; in particular, it equips the homotopy category of
\mathbf{2}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
with the structure of a symmetric monoidal closed category.

(3)

Each weak
3
-category is equivalent to a
Gray-category

[
22
]
: a category enriched in
(\mathbf{2}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p})
.

By virtue of (3), it suffices to work in a Gray-category rather than a weak
3
-category– see, for example,
[
15
]
. Gray-categories are more manageable than weak
3
-categories, and differ primarily from strict ones only in that the
middle four interchange
does not hold on the nose, but rather up to coherent isomorphism. For these reasons, Gray-categories are often called
semistrict

3
-categories.

Given this, it is natural to ask whether there exists an analogous symmetric monoidal closed structure on the category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
of Gray-categories satisfying similar good properties to the above ones. However, as argued by Crans in the introduction to
[
13
]
, it is impossible that there exists even a monoidal biclosed structure capturing weak transformations.

The obstruction is as follows. Suppose that
[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}]
is the internal hom for a monoidal biclosed structure, and suppose that its 1-cells
\eta\colon F\to G
are
weak transformations
. In particular, letting
\mathbf{2}=(0\to 1)
, the Gray-category
[\mathbf{2},\mathcal{B}]
would have arrows as its objects, and some kind of lax or pseudo-commuting squares as its
1
-cells, with pasting of these squares as composition.

Now
\eta\colon F\to G\in[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}]
can be viewed as a Gray-functor
\mathbf{2}\to[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}]
and so, by biclosedness, as a Gray-functor
\eta\colon\mathcal{A}\to[\mathbf{2},\mathcal{B}]
. This would send
x
to the component
\eta_{x}\colon Fx\to Gx
and
f\colon x\to y
to a lax square
\eta_{f}
as in the diagram below left; but now functoriality in
\mathcal{A}
would force the equation

(1)

to hold. But this equation, unnaturally strict at the
3
-dimensional level of Gray-categories, is in fact
impossible
— the failure of the middle-4-interchange in Gray-categories prevents such transformations from being composable.

A careful treatment of the above obstruction is given in
[
6
]
, which also shows that it is impossible to have a monoidal biclosed structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
interacting well with Lack’s model structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}

[
30
]
. These negative results indicate that if we wish to construct a homotopically well-behaved tensor product of Gray-categories, encoding an element of weakness appropriate to semistrict
4
-categories, then we should move outside the usual settings for enriched category theory — namely, symmetric monoidal closed and monoidal biclosed categories. But what sort of enriching structure might we look for?

Looking again at the above obstruction, we see that the problem stems from biclosedness, which forces weak transformations to be Gray-functors
\mathcal{A}\to[\mathbf{2},\mathcal{B}]
, and so forces Equation (
1
) to hold strictly. On the other hand, it would be more natural if this equation held only up to an invertible
3
-cell
\eta_{g,f}

(2)

and such a
3
-cell could be encoded by some sort of
weak map

\mathcal{A}\rightsquigarrow[\mathbf{2},\mathcal{B}]
. Given this, we might try abandoning strict Gray-functors and work with a category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
of Gray-categories and weak maps. However, this leads to new problems. Firstly, categories of weak maps are typically poorly behaved, lacking general limits and colimits. Consequently, even if we had a suitable internal hom
[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}]
on such a category, it is unlikely that we would be able to find a representing tensor product for it.

Therefore what we ultimately want is

•

a structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
encoding a notion of weak map
\mathcal{A}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal{B}
, in addition to a tensor product
\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
and internal hom
[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}]
, all interacting nicely.

Though not immediately apparent, the categorical structure that encodes these various features is that of a
closed skew monoidal category
. Skew monoidal categories were introduced by Szlachanyi in 2012
[
38
]
in the study of bialgebroids over rings and have since found applications in diverse areas, including
2
-category theory
[
7
]
, operad theory
[
31
]
, dg-categories
[
36
]
, cartesian differential categories
[
19
]
and theoretical computer science
[
2
]
. As with monoidal categories, they are categories equipped with a tensor product
\otimes\colon\mathcal{C}^{2}\to\mathcal{C}
and unit object
i
but now the coherence constraints are non-invertible and have the form

\alpha\colon(a\otimes b)\otimes c\to a\otimes(b\otimes c),\,l\colon i\otimes a\to a,\,r\colon a\to a\otimes i.

Whilst this choice seems a little arbitrary at first, it has a number of interesting consequences. For instance, the endofunctor
i\otimes-
and
-\otimes i
underlie a comonad and monad respectively, related by a distributive law. It follows that that each skew monoidal category encodes a notion of weak morphism
a\rightsquigarrow b
, defined as a morphism
i\otimes a\to b
in the Kleisli category for the comonad.

Similarly to the monoidal case, a skew monoidal category is closed if each
-\otimes a
has a right adjoint
[a,-]
. Much as in the classical context of Eilenberg-Kelly
[
16
]
, this yields a
skew closed category
in the sense of Street
[
37
]
, which involves a function

\mathcal{C}(a,b)\to\mathcal{C}(i,[a,b]).

Unlike in the classical setting, however, this is not necessarily invertible — indeed, as emphasised in
[
7
]
, the elements
i\to[a,b]
are the weak morphisms
i\otimes a\to b
, rather than just the
strict
morphisms
a\to b
of
\mathcal{C}
.

Here, we find the first hint of a connection between skew structures and
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
. In 2012, Gohla
[
20
]
described a notion of pseudomap
F\colon\mathcal{A}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal{B}
of Gray-categories and a so-called
mapping space

[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}]
, here called
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. These pseudomaps
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
are rather strict — as with normal pseudofunctors in
2
-category theory, the only weakening is an invertible coherence
2
-cell
F^{2}_{g,f}\colon F(g)F(f)\cong F(gf)
parametrised by a composable pair of
1
-cells
(f\colon x\to y,g\colon y\to z)
. In fact, this is just the coherence data that we need to introduce an invertible
3
-cell as in (
2
).

With regards the mapping-space
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, its objects are pseudomaps whilst the
1
-cells are
lax transformations
, which involve data
(\eta_{a},\eta_{f},\eta_{g,f})
as specified above, amongst further coherence data. We note that the lax transformations of
[
20
]
are
normal lax
, in the sense that they satisfy the normality condition that
\eta_{f}
is an identity if
f
is an identity.

Our first main goal is to prove the following result.

Theorem
5.8
.

There is a closed skew monoidal structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{l},1)
whose internal hom is
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

Our second goal is to prove an analogue of this result, involving a mapping space
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
of
pseudo-transformations
introduced here. In these, the
2
-cells
\eta_{f}
form part of specified adjoint equivalences satisfying further coherence equations. Our second main result is then:

Theorem
6.3
.

There is a closed skew monoidal structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},1)
whose internal hom is
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

Before diving into the paper, let us now give an outline of our approach to proving our main theorems. Given that they involve highly complex structures — see the appendix for the full axiomatics — a key challenge is not just to prove them, but to prove them clearly and efficiently. With this in mind, let us consider the various possible approaches to skew structures, and identify which will work best for our purpose. There are several essentially interchangable approaches, as drawn in the following schematic diagram.

Skew monoidal categories
Skew closed categories
Skew multicategories
4
-ary skew multicategories

The first approach would be to work with skew monoidal categories directly, constructing the skew monoidal structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
and showing that it is closed afterwards. Whilst the skew monoidal axioms are reasonably straightforward, the disadvantage is that tensor products are typically describable only via generators and relations, and not easy to work with directly.

The second approach would be to use skew closed categories
(\mathcal{C},[-,-],i)
, which involve coherence constraints
L\colon[b,c]\to[[a,b],[a,c]]
,
i\colon[i,a]\to a
and
j\colon i\to[a,a]

[
37
]
. Skew closed categories are said to be monoidal if each endofunctor
[a,-]
has a left adjoint and the resulting
monoidal skew closed categories
then amount to the same as closed skew monoidal categories. The advantage of focusing on the skew closed structure is that the internal hom, as in our present example, can often be described directly. The disadvantage is that the axiomatics, especially those involving
L
, are relatively unintuitive, and this can make constructing such a skew structure an ordeal. Following an explanation of how this should go by the first-named-author, in 2016 Gohla
[
21
]
made a start in following this approach in a more restrictive setting.
1
1

1

Gohla considered a version where
[A,B]
contains strict Gray-functors and a variant of pseudo-transformations involving invertible
2
-cells rather than adjoint equivalences.
He defined a
3
-graph map
L\colon[b,c]\to[[a,b],[a,c]]
between Gray-categories but verified its functoriality only in dimension
1
. Moreover, he did not verify naturality of
L
, nor describe the unit or unit maps, nor consider any of the axioms for a skew closed category.

A third approach to skew structures was introduced by the first-named-author and Lack in 2018
[
10
]
, namely
skew multicategories
. Skew multicategories are generalised multicategories with two kinds of multimap
A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\to B
, one called “tight” and the other “loose”. Amongst these, the left-representable closed skew multicategories again amount to the same as closed skew monoidal categories. The advantage of the multicategorical approach is that one can define multimaps in a direct way and the axioms are relatively straightforward. The disadvantage is that, unlike the other two concepts, which have finite definitions, here one has
n
-ary multimaps for all finite
n
, and infinitely many axioms to check (albeit, a finite axiom schema thereof). This is potentially problematic for us, since in our complex example, we wish to do as few calculations as possible.

Fortunately, this is not a fundamental problem. Indeed, since monoidal categories and representable multicategories are equivalent concepts
[
26
]
and since the former only require considering tensor products of four objects at a time, it is natural to expect that representable multicategories can be described in a way that involves only multimaps of at most dimension
4
. We call the resulting structures
4
-ary multicategories
and there is also a skew version. Again, each left-representable closed
4
-ary skew multicategory gives rise to a closed skew monoidal category and we will employ this result in proving our main theorems.

Having settled on our approach, let us now outline the construction of the
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
which is the technical heart of the paper.

•

Objects will be Gray-categories
\mathcal{A}
and nullary maps
a\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{A}
are objects of
\mathcal{A}
;

•

Tight and loose unary maps
\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
are Gray-functors and Gohla’s pseudomaps;

•

The
definitions
of tight and loose binary maps
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
are chosen so that they bijectively correspond to tight and loose unary maps
\lambda_{2}^{-1}(F)\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
into the mapping space;

•

Similarly, the
3
-ary and
4
-ary maps
F
will be defined so that they correspond to
2
-ary and
3
-ary maps
\lambda_{3}^{-1}F
and
\lambda_{4}^{-1}F
into the mapping space;

Building on work of Gohla
[

]
, we will show that his mapping space
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
extends to a bifunctor
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)
defined on pseudomaps. Transporting across the bijections
\lambda_{i}
, this enables us to define substitutions of unary maps with multimaps of all dimensions.

Of the remaining substitutions, the most important are the two substitutions of binary into binary. The first of these,

Substitution

Following this idea, the meat of our approach boils down to establishing the

and

for

. The remaining details, including the verification of the axioms are then completely straightforward.

Having outlined the construction of the
4
-ary skew multicategory, let us now give a more detailed overview of the paper. In Section
2
we introduce skew monoidal categories and the various flavours of multicategory that we will need, before describing the construction of a skew monoidal closed category from a
4
-ary skew multicategory satisfying the appropriate properties.

In Section
3
, we give some background on Gray-categories, before discussing Gohla’s pseudomaps and his lax mapping space
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, as well as an oplax variant
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. The technical heart of the paper is Section
4
, in which we construct the
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
. Studying its properties in Section
5
, we are able to prove, in Theorem
5.8
, our first main theorem — namely, the existence of the skew monoidal closed structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{l},1)
with internal hom
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

In Section
6
we establish analogous results to those above but replacing lax transformations by
pseudo-transformations
. In particular, in Theorem
6.3
we describe a skew monoidal closed structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},1)
with internal hom
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
containing pseudo-transformations as
1
-cells.

Finally in Section
7
, we use the notion of
sharp multimap
to show to refine the two aforementioned skew monoidal structures to
sharp
variations
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes^{\sharp}_{l},1)
and
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes^{\sharp}_{p},1)
whose associated internal homs
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{s}
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{s}
are the full sub-Gray-categories of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
containing the strict Gray-functors.

Further background and related work

In the 1990’s there began a significant stream of research on braided monoidal bicategories and semistrict braided monoidal 2-categories
[
27
,
3
,
15
,
12
,
24
]
, and it was recognised (see e.g.
[
3
]
) that the latter should be doubly degenerate
semistrict
4
-categories
.

A key player in this development was Crans, who began investigating the theory of semistrict
4
-categories. In
[
13
]
he described a monoidal structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
, intended as an analogue of the lax Gray-tensor product, which encodes certain lax transformations satisfying the problematic equation (
1
). Later in
[
14
]
he discussed a second monoidal structure, a pseudo variant of the aforementioned one, and defined
4
-teisi
(his semistrict
4
-categories) as categories enriched in it. However doubly degenerate
4
-teisi are stricter than semistrict braided monoidal 2-categories. Moreover, neither monoidal structure is closed (on either side) because of the problems concerning the equation (
1
) already discussed. This has the undesirable consequence that
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is not self-enriched with respect to either monoidal structure.

A more recent approach to semistrict
4
-categories is that of Bar and Vicary
[
4
]
who define
quasistrict 4-categories
, but no connection with enrichment has been made. Let us also mention the work of Batanin, Cisinski and Weber
[
5
]
which describes a tight relationship between normalised globular operads and lax monoidal structures, although this has not led to a definition of semistrict
4
-category.

Overview and future work

In the present paper, we move away from classical monoidal categories, as used by Crans
[
13
]
, to the skew monoidal categories of Szlachanyi
[
38
]
. Our main goal is to establish closed skew monoidal categories as the natural setting for enrichment on the category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
of Gray-categories, one capable of capturing weak higher dimensional transformations.

In a followup paper, we will focus primarily on the skew monoidal structures capturing pseudo-transformations, since these are the ones which are relevant to semistrict
4
-categories. We will investigate their interaction with Lack’s model structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}

[
30
]
, showing in particular that the sharp skew monoidal structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes^{\sharp}_{p},1)
induces a symmetric monoidal closed structure on the homotopy category of Gray-categories. Moreover, we will investigate categories enriched in these skew structures as semistrict 4-categories.

2.
Skew monoidal and multicategorical structures

In this section, we introduce the various categorical structures that we will use in the paper, beginning with skew monoidal categories. Following this, we discuss multicategories and skew multicategories, giving
k
-ary
— meaning,
k
-truncated — versions of both. Finally, we explain how
4
-ary skew multicategories satisfying certain properties give rise to closed skew monoidal categories.

2.1.
Skew monoidal categories

Skew monoidal categories were introduced by Szlachányi
[
38
]
in the study of bialgebroids over rings. A (left) skew monoidal category is a category
\mathcal{C}
together with a functor
\otimes\colon\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
, a unit object
i\in\mathcal{C}
, and natural families
\alpha\colon(a\otimes b)\otimes c\to a\otimes(b\otimes c)
,
l\colon i\otimes a\to a
and
r\colon a\to a\otimes i
satisfying five axioms described in
[
38
]
. We will not need the axioms here, but remark that they neatly correspond to the five words

abcd

iab

aib

abi

ii

of which the first corresponds to Mac Lane’s pentagon.

If the left unit map
l\colon i\otimes a\to a
is invertible for each
a
, then
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,i)
is said to be
left normal
. Dually, it is
right normal
if
r\colon a\to a\otimes i
is invertible for each
a
.
A monoidal category is precisely a skew monoidal category in which of the constraints
\alpha,l
and
r
are invertible.

Finally, a skew monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,i)
is said to be
closed
if each endofunctor
-\otimes a
has a right adjoint
[a,-]
.

2.2.
Classical and skew multicategories

There are two equivalent approaches to multicategories. In perhaps the better known of the two, one considers substitution in all variables simultaneously — see, for instance,
[
26
]
and
[
33
]
. On the other hand, the first approach to multicategories, due to Lambek
[
32
]
, focuses upon substitution in a single variable, as depicted below.

f
a
b
g
c
d
e

It is this approach that we will follow. In addition, we will make a refinement by defining the notion of a
k
-ary multicategory
, for
k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\omega\}
, which has multimaps of arity
n
only for natural numbers
n\leq k
. In particular,
\omega
-multicategories are just multicategories.

Definition 2.1
.

Let
k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\omega\}
. A
k

multicategory

\mathbb{C}
consists of

•

a collection of objects;

•

for each natural number

and list

\mathbb{C}_{n}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n};b)
of
n
-ary multimaps
;

•

for each object
a

1_{a}\in\mathbb{C}_{1}(a;a)
;

•

for natural numbers
n,m\leq k
with
n+m-1\leq k
and
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
a substitution function

(3)

\circ_{i}\colon\mathbb{C}_{n}(\overline{b};c)\times\mathbb{C}_{m}(\overline{a};b_{i})\to\mathbb{C}_{n+m-1}(\overline{b}_{<i},\overline{a},\overline{b}_{>i};c)

where
\overline{b}_{<i}
and
\overline{b}_{>i}

\overline{b}

, respectively.

For each

and

(4)

h\circ_{i}1_{b_{i}}=h\hskip 14.22636pt\textnormal{and}\hskip 14.22636pt1_{c}\circ h=h

(5)

\displaystyle h\circ_{i}(g\circ_{j}f)=(h\circ_{i}g)\circ_{j+i-1}f\hskip 14.22636pt

\displaystyle\textnormal{for}\hskip 14.22636pt1\leq i\leq m,1\leq j\leq n

(6)

\displaystyle(h\circ_{i}g)\circ_{n+j-1}f=(h\circ_{j}f)\circ_{i}g\hskip 14.22636pt

\displaystyle\textnormal{for}\hskip 14.22636pt1\leq i<j\leq m

for composable

of arity

respectively whenever these are defined (that is, when the four composites involved in each of these two equations have arity
\leq k
.)
2
2

2

The evident structure preserving morphisms between

Remark 2.2
.

Each
k
-ary multicategory has an underlying category
\mathbb{C}_{1}
with the same objects as
\mathbb{C}
and morphisms the unary ones. In particular, one can think of a
k
-ary multicategory as a category equipped with extra structure.

Substitution of unary and
n
-ary multimaps equips the sets
\mathbb{C}_{n}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n};b)
of
n
-ary multimaps with the structure of a functor

\mathbb{C}_{n}(-;-)\colon(\mathbb{C}_{1}^{n})^{op}\times\mathbb{C}_{1}\to\mathbf{Set}.

with respect to which the substitution maps
\circ_{i}\colon\mathbb{C}_{n}(\overline{b};c)\times\mathbb{C}_{m}(\overline{a};b_{i})\to\mathbb{C}_{n+m-1}(\overline{b}_{<i},\overline{a},\overline{b}_{>i};c)

are natural in each variable.

Observe that the category
\mathbb{C}_{1}
and functor
\mathbb{C}_{n}(-;-)
already encode all substitutions involving
n
-ary and unary morphisms, plus any associativity axioms involving two unary maps, as well as the unit axioms. The remaining associativity axioms involving a unary map are captured by naturality of the substitutions.

When constructing the
4
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}
in the next section, we will begin with a category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
, then construct the functors
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{n}(-;-)
of
n
-ary maps and the substitutions
\circ_{i}
, verifying that these are natural as we construct them, in this way verifying all associativity equations involving unary maps as well as the unit equations.

Skew multicategories were introduced in
[
10
]
. In general, these involve two types of multimorphisms, tight and loose, together with a function viewing tight multimaps as loose ones and satisfying some axioms. The concept simplifies significantly when these functions are subset inclusions and we will abuse the terminology by giving the definition under this restriction. Again, we give a
k
-ary version, with
\omega
-ary skew multicategories being the usual skew multicategories.

Definition 2.3
.

Let
k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\omega\}
. A
k
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
consists of a
k
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{C}^{l}
as above, whose multimaps we call
loose
, together with a subset
\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n};b)\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{l}_{n}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n};b)
for
1\leq n\leq k
of
tight

n
-ary multimaps.

Furthermore, we require that:

•

the unary identities in
\mathbb{C}^{l}
are tight;

•

the composite multimap
g\circ_{1}f
is tight whenever
g
and
f
are tight, and for
i\neq 1
, we require that
g\circ_{i}f
is tight whenever
g
is.

A multifunctor
F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
between
k
-ary skew multicategories is a multifunctor
F\colon\mathbb{C}^{l}\to\mathbb{D}^{l}
between the underlying
k
-ary multicategories of loose multimaps which preserves tightness of multimaps. These form the morphisms of the category
\mathbf{SkMult}_{k}
of
k
-ary skew multicategories.

In a
k
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
, the objects and tight morphisms form a subcategory
j\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}\to\mathbb{C}^{l}_{1}
of the category of loose unary morphisms. Note that a skew multicategory in which all loose multimaps are tight is precisely a multicategory.

Example 2.4
.

There is a multicategory
\mathbb{A}\mathbf{b}
of abelian groups, in which multimaps
F\colon A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\to B
are arbitrary functions
F\colon A_{1}\times\ldots\times A_{n}\to B
. It becomes a skew multicategory when, for
n\geq 1
, we say
F
is tight just when each
F(-,a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\colon A_{1}\to B
is a homomorphism of abelian groups — that is, it is a homomorphism in the first variable.

2.3.
Closedness

Let
k\geq 2
. A
k
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{C}
is said to be
closed
, if for all
b,c
, there exists an object
[b,c]
and binary map

e_{b,c}
[b,c]
b
c

for which the induced functions

e_{b,c}\circ_{1}-\colon\mathbb{C}_{n}(\overline{a};[b,c])\to\mathbb{C}_{n+1}(\overline{a},b;c)
are bijections for
0\leq n<k
. It is said to be
biclosed
if, moreover, there there exists an object
[b,c]^{\prime}
and binary map
e^{\prime}_{b,c}\colon b,[b,c]^{\prime}\to c
for which the induced functions
e^{\prime}_{b,c}\circ_{2}-\colon\mathbb{C}_{n}(\overline{a};[b,c])\to\mathbb{C}_{n+1}(b,\overline{a};c)
are bijections for
0\leq n<k
.

For a
k
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
to be
closed
, we firstly require that its
k
-ary multicategory of loose multimaps
\mathbb{C}^{l}
is closed. Furthermore, we require that
e_{b,c}\colon[b,c],b\to c
is tight and that the induced function
e_{b,c}\circ_{1}-\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n}(\overline{a};[b,c])\to\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n+1}(\overline{a},b;c)
is also a bijection for
1\leq n<k
. We will not consider biclosedness in the skew context since it does not feature in our examples.

Example 2.5
.

The skew multicategory
\mathbb{A}\mathbf{b}
is closed — the internal hom
[A,B]
is the abelian group of
functions
from
A
to
B
with addition and unit defined pointwise as in
B
.

2.4.
Left representability

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a
k
-ary skew multicategory where
k\geq 2
. A
tight binary map classifier
for
a
and
b
consists of a representation of
\mathbb{C}^{t}_{2}(a,b;-)\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}^{t}\to\mathbf{Set}
– in other words, a tight binary map

\theta_{a,b}
a
b
ab

for which the induced function
-\circ\theta_{a,b}\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(ab;c)\to\mathbb{C}^{t}_{2}(a,b;c)

is a bijection for all
c
. It is
left universal
if, moreover, the induced function

-\circ_{1}\theta_{a,b}\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n}(ab,\overline{c};d)\to\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n+1}(a,b,\overline{c};d)

is a bijection for all
n<k
and
\overline{c}
a tuple of the appropriate length.

Similarly, a
nullary map classifier is a representation of
\mathbb{C}^{l}_{2}(-;-)\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}\to\mathbf{Set}
— thus, a certain nullary map

u
i

in
\mathbb{C}
. It is
left universal
if, moreover, the induced function

-\circ_{1}u\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n+1}(i,\overline{c};d)\to\mathbb{C}^{l}_{n}(\overline{c};d)

is a bijection for each
n<k
and
\overline{c}
an
n
-tuple.

A
k
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
is said to be
left representable
if it admits left universal nullary and tight binary map classifiers.

2.5.
The closed left representable case

In the case that
\mathbb{C}
is closed, any nullary or tight binary map classifiers are
automatically left universal
. (Indeed, closedness allows us to remove the extra variable
\overline{x}
defining left universality by shifting it from the inputs of the multimap to the output.) Hence, a closed
k
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
is left representable just when it admits nullary and tight binary map classifiers.

Moreover, the internal homs assemble into an endofunctor
[b,-]\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}\to\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}
and the natural isomorphisms
\mathbb{C}^{t}_{2}(a,b;c)\cong\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(a;[b,c])
ensure that
\mathcal{C}
admits tight binary map classifiers just when each
[b,-]
has a left adjoint. Summing up,

•

a closed
k
-ary skew multicategory is left representable just when it admits a nullary map classifier and each endofunctor
[b,-]
has a left adjoint.

We will use this result in verifying left representability in our main examples. See Proposition 4.7 of
[
10
]
for a detailed proof in the case of skew multicategories, and note that the proof therein applies equally to the
k
-ary setting.

2.6.
4
-ary skew multicategories versus skew monoidal categories

In Section 6.2 of
[
10
]
, it was shown that left representable skew multicategories give rise to skew monoidal categories. Here we describe a truncated version of this result: namely, each left representable
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
gives rise to a skew monoidal structure on its underlying category
\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}
of tight unary maps. Let us now describe the associated skew monoidal structure — for a detailed verification of the axioms, we refer the reader to Lemma 4.5.8 of the second-named author’s Phd thesis
[
35
]
.

(1)

The tensor product of two objects
a,b\in\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}
is the tight binary map classifier
ab
whilst the unit
i
is the nullary map classifier.

(2)

Left representability ensures that the composite tight multimap below left

\theta_{a,b}
\theta_{ab,c}
ab
c
a
b
(ab)c

\theta_{b,c}
\theta_{a,bc}
a
bc
a(bc)
b
c

is a
tight
3
-ary map classifier
. By its universal property, the tight ternary map above right induces a unique tight unary morphism
\alpha\colon(ab)c\to a(bc)
which yields the rhs above under pre-composition with the lhs. This is the associator.

.

Remark 2.6
.

It appears that there is much more to say about
k
-ary multicategories — in particular, it seems that it is possible to complete each
k
-ary multicategory to a multicategory in a universal way (both in the ordinary and skew settings). Given that in the present paper we only need to consider
k
-ary skew multicategories for
k\leq 4
, we leave this to future developments.

3.
Pseudomorphisms and mapping spaces for Gray-categories

We begin the present section by reminding the reader about Gray-categories. Following Gohla
[
20
]
, we then define pseudomaps of Gray-categories and the mapping space
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
of lax transformations, establishing functoriality of
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)
on pseudomaps in Proposition
3.6
. We also introduce the Gray-category
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
of oplax transformations.

3.1.
Gray-categories

A Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
is a
(\mathbf{2}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},1)
-enriched category, where
\otimes_{p}
denotes the Gray-tensor product, as described in Section 3.2 of
[
25
]
or Section 4 of
[
22
]
. In particular, it amounts to:

(i)

A category
\mathcal{A}_{1}
of
0
and
1
-cells with composition of
f\colon x\to y
and
g\colon y\to z
denoted by
gf\colon x\to z
, and with identities denoted by
1_{x}\colon x\to x
.

(ii)

For
0
-cells
x,y
, a
2
-category
\mathcal{A}(x,y)
whose objects are the
1
-cells of
\mathcal{A}_{1}
, and whose
n
-cells are referred to as the
(n+1)
-cells of
\mathcal{A}
.

(iii)

Given
1
-cells
f\colon w\to x
and
g\colon y\to z
, there are
whiskering

2
-functors
-\circ f\colon\mathcal{A}(x,y)\to\mathcal{A}(w,y)
and
g\circ-\colon\mathcal{A}(x,y)\to\mathcal{A}(x,z)
whose action on objects is composition in
\mathcal{A}_{1}
. These whiskering operations are functorial in
\mathcal{A}_{1}
and compatible, in the sense that
(g\circ-)\circ f=g\circ(-\circ f)
.

(iv)

Given a pair of
2
-cells

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

there is an invertible
3
-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{2}f_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{2}f^{\prime}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{\prime}_{2}f_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{\prime}_{2}f^{\prime}_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}\circ\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi\circ f_{1}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi\circ f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}^{\prime}\circ\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi:\phi}

called the interchange map. The interchange maps satisfy several equations, for which we refer the reader to
[
17
, Definition 1.1]
.

In this section, for a Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
, we use
x,y,z,\ldots
to denote its 0-cells,

f_{1}\colon x\to y
,
f_{2}\colon x\to z
, …for its 1-cells,
\phi\colon f\to f^{\prime},\psi\colon g\to g^{\prime}\,\ldots
for 2-cells and
\Lambda\colon\alpha\to\alpha^{\prime}\,,\Theta\colon\beta\to\beta^{\prime}\,\ldots
for 3-cells. Compositions in the hom
2
-categories
\mathcal{A}(x,y)
will be denoted by

-\cdot-\colon\mathcal{A}(x,y)[g,h]\times\mathcal{A}(x,y)[f,g]\to\mathcal{A}(x,y)[f,h].

and we will use
\Lambda^{\prime}\ast\Lambda
for vertical composition of 3-cells in
\mathcal{A}(x,y)
.

We will rarely need any such notation, since composites in the hom-2-categories will almost always be given using diagrams. Our diagram style follows that of Gurski
[
25
]
. In diagrams, we will abuse notation for whiskering
2/3
-cells by a
1
-cell and only write
1\circ-
and
-\circ 1
, as in the diagram below. Finally, in some larger diagrams, where the context will make it clear, we will avoid labelling the interchange and only indicate it with a dashed double arrow again as in the diagram below.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{2}f_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{2}f^{\prime}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{\prime}_{2}f_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{\prime}_{2}f^{\prime}_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ\phi}

3.2.
Homomorphisms of Gray-categories

Given Gray-categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
, a Gray-functor
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
is a morphism of underlying
3
-graphs which preserves the Gray-category structure on the nose. We often refer to these Gray-functors as
strict maps
, and they form the morphisms of the category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
.

In
[
20
]
, Gohla defined the more general notion of a pseudo-Gray-functor
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
which we will call a
pseudomap
. A pseudomap
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
consists of a
3
-graph map together with a cocycle
F^{2}
, that is,

•

for any pair of 1-cells
f_{1}\colon x\to y
and
f_{2}\colon y\to z
in
\mathcal{A}
, an invertible 2-cell

F^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}\colon Ff_{2}\circ Ff_{1}\to F(f_{2}\circ f_{1})

in
\mathcal{B}
satisfying the nine axioms listed in
Section

A.1
.

We point out that pseudomaps preserve identity
1
-cells strictly and are very close to the notion of normal pseudofunctor in
2
-category theory.

Pseudomaps
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
and
G\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
can themselves be composed by composing the underlying functions on
3
-graphs and defining the invertible
2
-cell
(GF)^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}
to be the composite

\textstyle{GFf_{2}\circ GFf_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{G^{2}_{Ff_{2},Ff_{1}}}
\textstyle{G(Ff_{2}\circ Ff_{1})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{G(F^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}})}
\textstyle{GF(f_{2}\circ f_{1}).}

In this way, we obtain a category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
of Gray-categories and pseudomaps, which contains
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
as a subcategory via an identity on objects inclusion
j\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
.

Remark 3.1
.

As explained in Section 2 of
[
20
]
, the category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
is, in fact, the Kleisli category for a comonad
Q
on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
, with
j\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
the canonical inclusion to the Kleisli category. We now describe the comonad
Q
.

Given a Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
, consider its underlying category
\mathcal{A}_{1}
, and let
\epsilon\colon FU\mathcal{A}_{1}\to\mathcal{A}_{1}
denote the counit of the adjunction
F\dashv U
between categories and reflexive graphs. Here
FU\mathcal{A}_{1}
has objects as in
\mathcal{A}_{1}
and morphisms are of two kinds: (1) identities
1\colon x\to x\in\mathcal{A}_{1}
and (2) sequences of composable
non-identity
morphisms
\overline{f}=[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}]:x\to y
in
\mathcal{A}_{1}
where the domain of
f_{1}
is
x
and codomain of
f_{n}
is
y
. The functor
\epsilon\colon FU\mathcal{A}_{1}\to\mathcal{A}_{1}
sends composable sequences of morphisms to their composite. The counit
p\colon Q\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
of the comonad is the cartesian lifting of
\epsilon
along the forgetful functor
(-)_{0}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{Cat}
: in other words,
Q\mathcal{A}
has underlying category
FU\mathcal{A}_{1}
but has
Q\mathcal{A}(x,y)[\overline{f},\overline{g}]=\mathcal{A}(x,y)[\epsilon\overline{f},\epsilon\overline{g}]
— in particular,
p\colon Q\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
is fully faithful on 2-cells and 3-cells. Note that since
p
is identity on objects, full on
1
-cells and fully faithful both on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, it is a
triequivalence
of Gray-categories.

In referring to
Q
, we will call it the
pseudomap classifier comonad
. Indeed, its universal property from the Kleisli adjunction is that there is a universal pseudomap
q\colon\mathcal{A}\to Q\mathcal{A}
through which each pseudomap
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
factors uniquely as a strict map
F^{\prime}\colon Q\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
. The universal pseudomap
q\colon\mathcal{A}\to Q\mathcal{A}
is described as follows: it is the identity on objects, sends identity
1
-cells to identity
1
-cells, and sends non-identities
f\colon x\to y
to words
[f]\colon x\to y
. It is also the identity on
2
-cells and
3
-cells. The cocycle
q^{2}_{g,f}
is given by
1_{gf}\colon[g]\circ[f]\to[gf]
. We leave to the interested reader the construction of
F^{\prime}
, who can also refer for further details to Section 2 of
[
20
]
.

3.3.
Gohla’s mapping space of lax transformations

In
[
20
]
, Gohla defined a “mapping space” Gray-category
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
between Gray-categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
. Its cells in increasing dimension are pseudomaps, lax transformations, modifications and perturbations. We now spell out the data of the cells of each dimension, leaving the axioms to
Appendix

A
.

•

1-cells:
A
lax transformation

\alpha\colon F\to G
consists of:

–

For any object
x\in\mathcal{A}
, a 1-cell
\alpha_{x}\colon Fx\to Gx
in
\mathcal{B}
.

–

For any 1-cell
f\colon x\to y
in
\mathcal{A}
, a 2-cell in
\mathcal{B}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Fx}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gx}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Fy}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gy.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{x}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Ff}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Gf}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}}

–

For any 2-cell
\phi\colon f\to f^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
, a 3-cell
\alpha_{\phi}
in
\mathcal{B}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gf\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\alpha_{y}Ff}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gf^{\prime}\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\alpha_{y}Ff^{\prime}.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G\phi\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ F\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\phi}}

–

For any pair of 1-cells
f_{1}\colon x\to y
and
f_{2}\colon y\to z
in
\mathcal{A}
, an invertible 3-cell
\alpha^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}
in
\mathcal{B}
of the form

(7)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gf_{2}Gf_{1}\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gf_{2}\alpha_{y}Ff_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\alpha_{z}Ff_{2}Ff_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G(f_{2}f_{1})\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\alpha_{z}F(f_{2}f_{1}).}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ\alpha_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f_{2}}\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ F^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f_{2}f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}}

This data has to satisfy the seven axioms listed in
Section

A.2
.

•

2-cells:
A
modification

\Lambda\colon\alpha\to\beta
consists of:

–

For any object
x\in\mathcal{A}
, a 2-cell
\Lambda_{x}\colon\alpha_{x}\to\beta_{x}
in
\mathcal{B}
.

–

For any 1-cell
f\colon x\to y
in
\mathcal{A}
, a 3-cell
\Lambda_{f}
in
\mathcal{B}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gf\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Gf\beta_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\alpha_{y}Ff}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\beta_{y}Ff.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ\Lambda_{x}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lambda_{y}\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lambda_{f}}

This data has to satisfy the three axioms listed in
Section

A.3
.

•

3-cells:
A
perturbation

\theta\colon\Lambda\to\Gamma
consists of, for any object
x\in\mathcal{A}
, a 3-cell
\theta_{x}\colon\Lambda_{x}\to\Gamma_{x}
in
\mathcal{B}
subject to the axiom in
Section

A.4
.

The Gray-category structure on
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
was constructed in
[
20
]
and is described explicitly in
Appendix

B
.

It follows immediately from this description that there are evaluation Gray-functors
ev_{x}\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathcal{B}
where
x
is an object of
\mathcal{A}
: here,
ev_{x}
sends a pseudomap
F
to its value
Fx
, a lax transformation
\alpha
to its component
\alpha_{x}
, a modification
\Gamma
to the
2
-cell
\Gamma_{x}
and a perturbation to the
3
-cell
\theta_{x}
. Since perturbations are merely indexed families of
3
-cells, it is immediate that the evaluation maps
ev_{x}\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathcal{B}
are jointly faithful on
3
-cells.

Remark 3.2
.

Whilst we have given a direct description of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
above, we note that Gohla takes a more abstract approach beginning by constructing a
path space
functor
P\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
. He then employs iterated powers of
P
to obtain the general mapping spaces
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. We describe the construction in more detail in Remark
5.5
.

3.4.
The mapping space bifunctor
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)

In Section 6 of
[
20
]
, Gohla describes functoriality properties of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
in
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
, which we now review and then extend.

•

Firstly, given a
pseudomap

F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
there is, by Theorem 6.2 of
[
20
]
, a
strict
map
\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B})\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.
On
0
-cells this is given by pre-composition by
F
and on higher cells it is given by left whiskering. Full details are given in
Section

C.1
.

•

Secondly, given a
strict map

G\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
, there is, by Theorem 6.4 of
[
20
]
, a strict map
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
. On
0
-cells this is given by post-composition by
G
and on
1/2/3
-cells it is given by right whiskering. Right whiskering by
G
simply applies the strict map
G
to the components of the relevant lax transformation/modification or perturbation.

These operations yield functors
\mathbf{Lax}(-,\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)
and using the description of
\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B})
in
Section

C.1
together with the action of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
by application, it is trivial to verify the compatibility
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B})=\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B}^{\prime})\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},G)
so producing a bifunctor
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
.

For our purposes, we need to extend this to a bifunctor
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
, which requires constructing a pseudomap
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
for each pseudomap
G\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
. Again, this is given by right whiskering, but this is now more subtle, involving conjugation by the invertible cocyle
G^{2}
. We give full explicit details of these right whiskering operations in
Section

C.2
, for instance, describing the data of the whiskered lax transformation
G\alpha
.

However, it would be rather tedious to give a direct verification using these formulae that
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
is a pseudomap — for instance, we would need to verify that
G\alpha
, so defined, satisfies the axioms for a lax transformation. Therefore, we now provide a conceptual construction of the pseudomap
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
which avoids any such calculations. (This approach is guided by the theory of weak maps for algebraic weak factorisation systems
[
9
]
, but we will keep our treatment essentially elementary, leaving a full treatment of the algebraic aspects as an option for the reader in the proof of Proposition
3.6
.)

To this end, let us define an
algebraic surjection
to be a strict map
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
of Gray-categories which is surjective on
0
-cells, full on
1
-cells, fully faithful on both
2
-cells and
3
-cells and, moreover, equipped with a
lifting function

\phi
giving:

•

for each
x\in\mathcal{B}
, an object
\phi x\in\mathcal{A}
such that
G(\phi x)=x
;

•

for each
x,y\in\mathcal{A}
and
1
-cell
f\colon Gx\to Gy\in\mathcal{B}
, a
1
-cell
\phi(x,f,y)\colon x\to y
such that
G\phi(x,f,y)=f
and satisfying the normality condition
\phi(x,1_{Gx},x)=1_{x}
.

We denote an algebraic surjection as above by
(F,\phi)\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
and sometimes abuse notation by writing
\phi(f)\colon x\to y
instead of
\phi(x,f,y)
when the context is clear.

We remark that algebraic surjections are trivial fibrations for Lack’s model structure on Gray-categories
[
30
]
, but have the stronger property of being faithful on
2
-cells.

Example 3.3
.

The counit
p\colon Q\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
is an algebraic surjection, when equipped with the structure
\phi x=x
on objects and, on maps
f
,
\phi(x,f,y)=[f]
if
f
is non-identity and
\phi(x,f,y)=1_{x}
if it is the identity.

Lemma 3.4
.

Each algebraic surjection
(F,\phi)\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
has a canonical section
F_{\phi}\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}
in
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
.

Proof.

On objects, we set
F_{\phi}x=\phi(x)
and, at
f\colon x\to y
, we define
F_{\phi}f=\phi(f)\colon F_{\phi}x\to F_{\phi}y
so that
F(F_{\phi}x)=x
and
F(F_{\phi}f)=f
. By the normality condition for
\phi
,
F_{\phi}
preserves identity
1
-cells. Since
F
is fully faithful on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, there exists a unique way in which to complete
F_{\phi}
to a morphism of
3
-graphs such that
FF_{\phi}=1
. In fact, there is a unique way to complete
F_{\phi}
to a pseudomap such that
FF_{\phi}=1
. Indeed, given
1
-cells
f\colon x\to y
and
g\colon y\to z
we obtain the parallel
1
-cells
F_{\phi}g\circ F_{\phi}f,F_{\phi}(g\circ f)\colon F_{\phi}x\rightrightarrows F_{\phi}z
in
\mathcal{A}
both of which are sent by
F
to
g\circ f
; by
2
-fully faithfulness of
F
on
2
-cells, there exists a unique invertible
2
-cell
(F_{\phi})^{2}_{g,f}\colon F_{\phi}g\circ F_{\phi}f\Rightarrow F_{\phi}(g\circ f)
such that
F(F_{\phi})^{2}_{g,f}=1
.

It remains to verify the pseudomap equations for
F_{\phi}
. Having verified that
F_{\phi}
preserves identity
1
-cells, all of the remaining equations concern equalities between parallel
2
-cells or
3
-cells in
\mathcal{A}
. Since
F
is faithful on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, it suffices to show that each of these equations hold after application of
F
, whereupon they are sent to the corresponding equation for
FF_{\phi}
to be a pseudomap. And these hold since
FF_{\phi}
is the identity on
\mathcal{B}
.
∎

Lemma 3.5
.

Given an algebraic surjection
(F,\phi)\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
, we obtain an algebraic surjection
(\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},F),\phi^{\mathcal{C}})\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B})
.

Proof.

Given a pseudomap
G\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}
we set
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}(G)=F_{\phi}\circ G\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}
, noting that
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},F)F_{\phi}\circ G=F\circ F_{\phi}\circ G=G
as required.

At a lax transformation
\alpha\colon FG\to FH
, we must construct a lax transformation
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha\colon G\to H
. At
x\in\mathcal{C}
, we define
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{x}=\phi(\alpha_{x})\colon Gx\to Hx
. At
f\colon x\to y\in\mathcal{A}
, we use
2
-fully faithfulness of
F
to define
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{f}\colon Gf\circ\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{x}\Rightarrow\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{y}\circ Ff
as the unique
2
-cell such that
F\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{f}=\alpha_{f}
; similarly, we use
3
-fully faithfulness to define the invertible
3
-cells
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{\phi}
and
(\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha)^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}
as the unique
3
-cells with the appropriate domain and codomain such that
F(\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha_{\phi})=\alpha_{\phi}
and
F((\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha)^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}})=\alpha^{2}_{f_{2},f_{1}}
.

All of the equations for
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha
involve equalities of parallel
2
-cells and
3
-cells; since
F
is fully faithful on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, it suffices to show that these equations hold under application of
F
, under which, they become the corresponding equations for the lax transformation
\alpha
.

We must also verify that if
\alpha
is the identity, then so is
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha
, but this follows from normality of
\phi
and fully faithfulness of
F
on
2
-cells and
3
-cells.

Since
F
is fully faithful on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, and since modifications and perturbations are defined using only
2
-cells and
3
-cells,
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},F)
is also fully faithful on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, completing the proof that it is an algebraic surjection.

∎

Now consider a pseudomap
G\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
. By the universal property of the pseudomap classifier
Q\mathcal{B}
, there exists a unique strict map
G^{\prime}\colon Q\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
such that
G^{\prime}\circ q=G
. Now by Example
3.3
,
(p,\phi):Q\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}
is an algebraic surjection; hence by
Lemma

3.5
so is
(\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},p),\phi^{\mathcal{C}})
; therefore, by
Lemma

3.4
, we obtain a pseudomap
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},p)_{\phi^{\mathcal{C}}}\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},Q\mathcal{B})
. Therefore, we define
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
as the composite pseudomap

(8)

\textstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},p)_{\phi^{\mathcal{C}}}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},Q\mathcal{B})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G^{\prime})}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}).}

Unpacking this definition yields the explicit description of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
given in
Section

C.2
. Note that if
G
is strict,
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
is just the strict map given by direct application of
G
. With this in place, let us state the main result of this section.

Proposition 3.6
.

We obtain a functor
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
such that
\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B})
is always strict and
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
is strict whenever
G
is.

Proof.

It remains to verify that
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)
preserves composition and satisfy the compatibility
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B})=\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B}^{\prime})\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},G)
. There are two approaches.

The first is elementary — these equations follow from a few straightforward calculations using the explicit description of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
in
Section

C.2
. We leave this approach to the interested reader.

The second approach builds upon the conceptual definition of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
using algebraic surjections, and makes serious use of the theory of algebraic weak factorisation systems (awfs), and in particular results from
[
8
]
and
[
9
]
. For the reader with a good knowledge of awfs, we describe this proof now. We will freely use notation and terminology from
[
8
]
and
[
9
]
.

To this end, the starting observation is that there is a small subcategory
\mathcal{J}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}^{{\mathbf{2}}}
of the category of morphisms such that algebraic surjections are morphisms equipped with a lifting operation against
\mathcal{J}
in the sense of
[
18
]
. Though the details are not needed, we note that
\mathcal{J}
contains as objects the generating cofibrations for Lack’s model structure on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}

[
30
]
, plus a further one encoding that algebraic surjections are faithful on
2
-cells. Finally, in order to encode the normality condition, we add
id_{1}\colon 1\to 1
to
\mathcal{J}
together with the unique morphism
j\to id_{1}
where
j
is the generating cofibration encoding fullness on
1
-cells.

It follows that algebraic surjections form a concrete double category
\mathbb{S}\mathbf{urj}\to\mathbb{S}\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat})
in the sense of

]
, where

and

the forgetful double functor. It is easy to describe it directly. The objects and horizontal morphisms of
\mathbb{S}\mathbf{urj}
are those of
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
. The vertical morphisms are the algebraic surjections, whilst the squares are commuting squares as below

\textstyle{\mathcal{A}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{C}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{B}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{D}}
\scriptstyle{R}
\scriptstyle{(F,\phi)}
\scriptstyle{(G,\theta)}
\scriptstyle{S}

which commute with the lifting functions
\phi

and

, the composite algebraic surjection

with formulae
\theta*\phi(x)=\phi(\theta(x))
and
(\theta*\phi)(x,f,y)=\phi(x,\theta(Fx,f,Fy),y)
.

Since
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is locally presentable and
\mathcal{J}
is small, by Proposition 23 of

with concrete double category of right maps

\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}

, whose value at

In fact, this

: that is, given an algebraic surjection

and morphism

, we must show that there exists a unique morphism of algebraic surjections as depicted below

\textstyle{Q\mathcal{A}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{B}}

\textstyle{\mathcal{C}}
\scriptstyle{K}

. On morphisms, consider a generating non-identity

. Since

Having established that the pseudomorphism classifier

\textstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

is a morphism of algebraic surjections. At

. We will show that given an algebraic surjection

, the commutative square

\textstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},F),\phi^{\mathcal{C}})}

\textstyle{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{A})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

, as described in Theorem 10 of

At

the lifting
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}(X)
is, by definition, the composite
F_{\phi}X\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}
. Likewise the lifting

. As such, associativity

in
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
ensures that the square commutes with lifting functions on objects. At a lax transformation
\alpha\colon FX\to FY\in\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B})
, we have the lifting
\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha\colon X\to Y\in\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})
. We must prove that we have an equality of lax transformations
(\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha)G=\phi^{\mathcal{C}}(\alpha G):XG\to YG
. Since both are sent by the strict morphism
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},F)
to
\alpha G
, and since the algebraic surjection
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},F)
is faithful both on
2
-cells and
3
-cells, it suffices to show that
(\phi^{\mathcal{C}}\alpha)_{Gx}=\phi^{\mathcal{C}}(\alpha G)_{x}
at each
0
-cell
x
of
\mathcal{C}
. By definition, both have value
\phi(\alpha_{Gx})\colon XGx\to YGx
, as required.

∎

3.5.
Oplax transformations

In order to define the Gray-category
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
of oplax transformations, it will be convenient to use duality. To this end, given a Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
, we write
\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}}
for the Gray-category whose
2
-cells are reversed, but whose
0,1
and
3
-cells have the same orientation.

There is an isomorphism of categories
(-)^{co}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
sending
\mathcal{A}
to

and sending a pseudomap

to the pseudomap

in which:

•

has the same action on

and
3
-cells.

•

in

in
\mathcal{B}
.

With this in place, let us define

4.
The
4
-ary skew multicategory of Gray-categories and lax multimaps

In this section, we construct a

-ary skew multicategory

whose category of loose unary maps is
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
, and whose category of tight unary maps is

. Our approach is to build it from the bottom up, first building a

4
-ary skew multicategory.

.

4.1.
Nullary maps

The set
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})
of nullary maps is defined to be the set of objects of
\mathcal{A}
. Given
a\in\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})
and a pseudomap
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
we define
F\circ a:=Fa
.
This equips the set of nullary maps with the action of a functor
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{Set}
.

4.2.
Unary maps

We set
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{1}(-;-):=\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}(-,-)
— the loose unary maps are the pseudomaps, with their substitution given by composition in
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
. The set
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{t}_{1}(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{B})
of tight unary maps consists of the Gray-functors. The identities are tight and composite
G\circ_{1}F
of two tight maps is tight, since
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is a subcategory of
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
.

Let us note that we have the following trivial result, relating nullary and unary maps, which is our first indication of closedness.

Lemma 4.1
.

There is a bijection
\lambda_{1}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{1}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, natural in each variable.

Proof.

\lambda_{1}
is in fact the identity in each component.
∎

4.4.
The correspondence between binary and unary maps

In order to equip the sets
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
of loose binary maps with the structure of a functor

\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(-,-;-)\colon(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{2})^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{Set}

we will use the following result, which again forms part of closedness.

Proposition 4.2
.

There is a bijection
\lambda_{2}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{l}(\mathcal{A};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
which restricts to tight maps on both sides.

Proof.

The data for a pseudomap
\overline{F}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
is a
3
-graph map together with invertible
2
-cells
\overline{F}^{2}_{A_{2},A_{1}}\colon\overline{F}(A_{2})\overline{F}(A_{1})\cong\overline{F}(A_{2}A_{1})
. Let us firstly check that this data is in correspondence with the data for a binary map.

(1)

On objects, it assigns to
a\in\mathcal{A}
a pseudomap
\overline{F}(a)=F^{a}
. This involves
5
pieces of data:
F^{a}(b)
,
F^{a}(B)
,

and

(here we are using notation consistent with the diagrams in

).

(2)

we obtain a lax transformation

. This involves four pieces of data: a

4.5.
Compact definition for binary maps

We can give an equivalent description of loose binary maps using just pseudomaps, lax and oplax transformations and modifications. In these terms, a loose binary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
consists of:

(1.1)

at an object
a\in\mathcal{A}
, a pseudomap
F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
,

(1.2)

at an object
b\in\mathcal{B}
, a pseudomap
F_{b}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}
,

such that
F^{a}(b)=F_{b}(a)
, together with:

(2.1)

at a 1-cell
A\colon a\to a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
, a lax transformation
F^{A}\colon F^{a}\to F^{a^{\prime}}
,

(2.2)

at a 1-cell
B\colon b\to b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}
, an oplax transformation
F_{B}\colon F_{b}\to F_{b^{\prime}}
,

such that

F^{A}(b)=F_{b}(A)
,
F_{B}(a)=F^{a}(B)
,

(F^{A})_{B}=(F_{B})_{A}=:A_{B}
.

Moreover we require the data

(F^{\alpha})_{b}:=F_{b}(\alpha)
,
(F^{\alpha})_{B}:=F_{B}(\alpha)
,

(F_{\beta})^{a}:=F^{a}(\beta)
,
(F_{\beta})^{A}:=(F^{A})_{\beta}
,

(F^{A_{2},A_{1}})^{b}:=(F_{b})^{A_{2},A_{1}}
,
(F^{A_{2},A_{1}})^{B}:={(F_{B})^{A_{2},A_{1}}}
,

(F_{B_{2},B_{1}})^{a}:=(F^{a})_{B_{2},B_{1}}
,
{(F_{B_{2},B_{1}})^{A}}:=(F^{A})_{B_{2},B_{1}}
,

to form two modifications

F^{\alpha}\colon F^{A}\to F^{A^{\prime}}
in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
,

F_{\beta}\colon F_{B}\to F_{B^{\prime}}
in
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})
,

and two invertible modifications

F^{A_{2},A_{1}}\colon F^{A_{2}}\cdot F^{A_{1}}\to F^{A_{2}A_{1}}
in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
,

F_{B_{2},B_{1}}\colon F_{B_{2}}\cdot F_{B_{1}}\to F_{B_{2}B_{1}}
in
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})
.

We refer to this as the
compact definition
for loose binary maps. Let us compare it with the earlier definition. Both begin with pseudomaps
F^{a}
and
F_{b}
. Clearly the axioms for

\mathcal{B}
,
F_{\Theta}\colon F_{\beta}\to F_{\beta^{\prime}}
in
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})
,

with components defined as

(F^{\Lambda})_{b}:=F_{b}(\Lambda)
and
(F_{\Theta})_{a}:=F^{a}(\Theta)
.

The equation for
F^{\Lambda}
to be a perturbation corresponds to Axiom (
ii
) for the oplax transformation
F_{B}
and the equation for
F_{\Theta}
corresponds to Axiom (
ii
) for the lax transformation
F^{A}
.

4.6.
The functor of binary maps

Consider again the bijection

\lambda_{2}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{l}(\,\mathcal{A};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\,)\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})

of Proposition
4.2
, which restricts to tight maps on either side. The left hand side of the above bijection is functorial in
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
— hence the sets
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
on the right hand side extend uniquely to a functor

\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(-,-;-)\colon(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{2})^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{Set}

such that the bijection
\lambda_{2}
is natural in each variable.

This immediately defines the substitutions of loose unary and binary. Using that
\lambda_{2}
restricts to tight maps, plus the behaviour of
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)
with respect to tight morphisms, as per Proposition
3.6
, we obtain that
F\circ_{1}P
is tight if
F
and
P
are,
F\circ_{2}Q
is tight if
F
is, and
R\circ_{1}F
is tight if both
G
and
F
are, where
F
is a binary map and
R,P
and
Q
unary.

We spell out the details of these three substitutions in
Table

3
using the compact definition of binary maps described in
Section

4.5
.

Table 3
.
Substitutions in compact form

F\circ_{1}P

(F\circ_{1}P)^{a}=F^{Pa}

(F\circ_{1}P)_{b}=F_{b}\circ P

(F\circ_{1}P)^{A}=F^{PA}

(F\circ_{1}P)_{B}=F_{B}\circ P

F\circ_{2}Q

(F\circ_{2}Q)^{a}=F^{a}\circ Q

(F\circ_{2}Q)_{b}=F_{Qb}

(F\circ_{2}Q)^{A}=F^{A}\circ Q

(F\circ_{2}Q)_{B}=F_{QB}

G\circ_{1}F

(G\circ_{1}F)^{a}=G\circ F^{a}

(G\circ F)_{b}=G\circ F_{b}

(G\circ_{1}F)^{A}=G\circ F^{A}

(G\circ F)_{B}=G\circ F_{B}

4.7.
The duality isomorphism in dimension
2

Proposition 4.4
.

There is a bijection

d^{2}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}};\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}}),

natural in each variable.

Proof.

Given
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
, we start by constructing
d^{2}F\colon\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{A}^{co}\to\mathcal{C}^{co}
and, to this end, will use the compact definition of binary map.

•

At
b\in\mathcal{B}^{co}
, we define
d^{2}F^{b}=(F_{b})^{co}\colon\mathcal{A}^{co}\to\mathcal{C}^{co}
;

•

at
a\in\mathcal{A}^{co}
, we define
d^{2}F_{a}=(F^{a})^{co}\colon\mathcal{B}^{co}\to\mathcal{C}^{co}
;

and we observe that
d^{2}F^{b}(a)=F_{b}(a)=F^{a}(b)=d^{2}F_{a}(b)
as required. Next,

•

at
B\colon b\to b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}^{co}
, we define
d^{2}F^{B}\colon d^{2}F^{b}\to d^{2}F^{b^{\prime}}
as the lax transformation
(F_{B})^{+}\colon(F_{b})^{co}\to(F_{b^{\prime}})^{co}
;

•

at
A\colon a\to a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{co}
, we define
d^{2}F_{A}\colon d^{2}F_{a}\to d^{2}F_{a^{\prime}}
as the oplax transformation
({F^{A}})^{-}\colon(F^{a})^{co}\to(F^{a^{\prime}})^{co}
.

This describes the data for
d^{2}F
. The equation
d^{2}F^{B}(a)=d^{2}F_{a}(B)
holds since we have
(F_{B})^{+}(a)=F_{B}(a)=F^{a}(B)=(F^{a})^{-}(B)
. Similarly
d^{2}F_{A}(b)=(d^{2}F^{b})(A)
and
(d^{2}F^{B})_{A}=(d^{2}F^{B})_{A}
reduce to the corresponding equations
F^{A}(b)=F_{b}(A)
and
(F_{B})_{A}=(F^{A})_{B}
for
F
.
Lastly, we must prove that the data

d^{2}F^{\beta}
,
d^{2}F_{\alpha}
,
d^{2}F^{B_{2},B_{1}}
and
d^{2}F_{A_{2},A_{1}}
as defined in Section
4.5
yield modifications; but these are simply the modifications
(F_{\beta})^{+}
,
(F^{\alpha})^{-}
,
(F_{B_{2},B_{1}})^{+}
and
(F^{A_{2},A_{1}})^{-}
respectively, proving that
d^{2}F
is a binary map.

Naturality of
d^{2}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}
in each variable follows formally using only the compact definitions of substitution, as per
Table

3
, plus functoriality of
(-)^{co}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
together with naturality of
{(-)^{+}}
and
(-)^{-}
.

Observe that since
(-)^{+}
and
(-)^{-}
are inverse operations, it follows directly that
d^{2}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}};\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}})
has inverse

d^{2}_{\mathcal{A}^{co},\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co}}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}};\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C}).

In particular,
d^{2}
is a natural bijection.
∎

4.8.
Substitution of nullary into binary

At
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
and
a\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{A}
we define
F\circ_{1}a:=F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
; similarly, at
b\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{B}
, we define
F\circ_{2}b=F_{b}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}
. By construction
F\circ_{2}b
is tight if
F
is.
Naturality of
\circ_{1}
and
\circ_{2}
follow from the description of substitution of loose unary and binary in
Table

3
. All of the cases are similar. For instance, consider
b\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
together with
Q
and
F
as in
Table

3
. Then

(F\circ_{2}Q)\circ_{2}b=(F\circ_{2}Q)_{b}=F_{Qb}
whilst
F\circ_{2}(Q\circ_{1}b)=F\circ_{2}Qb=F_{Qb}
using only definitional equalities and the description of
F\circ_{2}Q
in the table.

In Proposition
4.6
, we will also make of the following simple lemma.

Lemma 4.5
.

Given a nullary map
a\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{A}
and unary map
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
the equality
\lambda_{1}(F\circ_{1}a)=\lambda_{2}(F)\circ_{1}a\in\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
holds.

Proof.

By definition of
\lambda_{1}
and of substitution of nullary into unary, we have
\lambda_{1}(F\circ_{1}a)=F(a)
. We also have
\lambda_{2}(F)\circ_{1}a=\lambda_{2}(F)^{a}=F(a)
where the first equation holds by definition of substitution of nullary into binary and the second equation holds by definition of
\lambda_{2}(F)\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
as per
4.2
.
∎

4.9.
A
2
-ary skew multicategory

We have defined all of the structure for the
2
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
and verified all associativity equations involving unary maps. The only case left to consider is the associativity equation
(F\circ_{1}a)\circ_{1}b=(F\circ_{2}b)\circ_{1}a
for a binary map and two nullary maps. This is simply the binary map equation
F^{a}(b)=F_{b}(a)
.

4.10.
Ternary maps

A
loose ternary map

F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
consists of:

(1)

at an object
a\in\mathcal{A}
a loose binary map
F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
, at
b\in\mathcal{B}
a loose binary map
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
and at
c\in\mathcal{C}
a loose binary map
F_{c}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{D}
such that

F^{a}(b,-)=F\hbox{}\,\vbox{\Let@\restore@math@cr\default@tag\halign{\if cl\else\hfil\fi$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\if cr\else\hfil\fi&&\thickspace\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\mathstrut\\
\mathstrut b\\
\mathstrut\crcr}}\,(a,-)=:F^{a}_{b}\quad F^{a}(-,c)=F_{c}(a,-)=:F^{a}_{c}

F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(-,c)=F_{c}(-,b)=:F^{b}_{c}
,

(2)

at 1-cells
A\colon a\to a^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
,
B\colon b\to b^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{B}
and
C\colon c\to c^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{C}
, a 3-cell
F^{a^{\prime}}_{b^{\prime}}(C)F^{a^{\prime}}_{c}(B)F^{b}_{c}(A)
F^{a^{\prime}}_{c^{\prime}}(B)F^{a^{\prime}}_{b}(C)F^{b}_{c}(A)
F^{a^{\prime}}_{b^{\prime}}(C)F^{b^{\prime}}_{c}(A)F^{a}_{c}(B)
F^{b^{\prime}}_{c^{\prime}}(A)F^{a}_{b^{\prime}}(C)F^{a}_{c}(B)
F^{a^{\prime}}_{c^{\prime}}(B)F^{b}_{c^{\prime}}(A)F^{a}_{b}(C)
F^{b^{\prime}}_{c^{\prime}}(A)F^{a}_{c^{\prime}}(B)F^{a}_{b}(C)
,
{A_{B}}^{c^{\prime}}\circ 1
{B_{C}}^{a^{\prime}}\circ 1
1\circ{A_{B}}^{c}
1\circ{A_{C}}^{b}
{A_{C}}^{b^{\prime}}\circ 1
1\circ{B_{C}}^{a}
(A\mid B\mid C)

which we call the
incubator
, satisfying the nine axioms described in
Section

D.2
.

We say that the loose ternary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
is tight if
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{D}
and
F_{c}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
are tight.

4.11.
The correspondence between ternary and binary maps

Proposition 4.6
.

There is a bijection
\lambda_{3}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{3}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C};\mathcal{D})
, which restricts to tight maps on both sides.

Proof.

Consider a binary map
\overline{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
. This is specified by the following data:

(1)

Pseudomaps
\overline{F}^{a}\colon\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
and
\overline{F}_{b}\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
;

(2)

a modification
A_{B}\colon\overline{F}^{a^{\prime}}(B)\cdot\overline{F}_{b}(A)\to\overline{F}_{b^{\prime}}(A)\cdot\overline{F}^{a}(B)
in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
;

(3)

four perturbations
\alpha_{B}
,
A_{\beta}
,
\overline{F}^{A_{2},A_{1}}_{B}
,
\overline{F}^{A}_{B_{2},B_{1}}\in\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
, the latter two invertible;

all satisfying the binary map equations. Now, we will describe the associated ternary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
. It is convenient, for fixed objects
a,b,c
to consider the diagram

(10)

since it encodes the three binary maps we wish to construct and the three equations relating them. Firstly, the two pseudomaps
\overline{F}^{a}=\overline{F}\circ_{1}a
and
\overline{F}_{b}=\overline{F}\circ_{2}b
correspond under the bijection
\lambda_{2}
of Proposition
4.2
to binary maps
F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D},F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
. Also, for each
c\in\mathcal{C}
we have the composite binary map
F_{c}:=ev_{c}\circ_{1}F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\to\mathcal{D}
.

Next, we must verify that these satisfy the three compatibility equations for a ternary map. To this end, observe that the associativity equation
(ev_{c}\circ_{1}\overline{F})\circ_{1}a=ev_{c}\circ_{1}(\overline{F}\circ_{1}a)
in the
2
-multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
is precisely the equality of pseudomaps
F^{a}(-,c)=F_{c}(a,-)
. Likewise the associativity
(ev_{c}\circ_{1}\overline{F})\circ_{2}b=ev_{c}\circ_{1}(\overline{F}\circ_{2}b)
yields
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(-,c)=F_{c}(-,b)
. Finally, consider the associativity equation
(\overline{F}\circ_{1}a)\circ_{1}b=(\overline{F}\circ_{2}b)\circ_{1}a
. Applying
\lambda_{1}
to both sides and using Lemma
4.5
, this equation becomes the required equality of pseudomaps
F^{a}(b,-)=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(a,-)
.

Consider the modification
A_{B}
in (2) above. Its component at
c\in\mathcal{C}
is encoded in the binary map
F_{c}
. On the other hand, the value of
A_{B}
at a
1

is a
3
-cell not encoded by any of the three binary maps — this is the extra piece of data, the incubator
(A|B|C)
.

The four perturbations in (3) are specified by their components for each
c\in\mathcal{C}
and so encoded by the binary maps
F_{c}
.

Finally we turn to the axioms, detailed in
Table

. Firstly, there are the three equations for
A_{B}
to be a modification. Next, there is the single perturbation equation for each of the four perturbations in (3) above. Then we are left with the binary map equations for

4.12.

Consider again the bijection

\lambda_{3}
is natural in each variable.

This immediately defines the substitution of loose ternary and loose unary maps. Furthermore, the behaviour of

, ensures that

F

Proposition 4.7
.

There is a bijection

.

To get started, we set

\overline{F}^{c}:=d^{2}(F_{c}),\overline{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}:=d^{2}(F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}})\textnormal{ and }\overline{F}_{a}:=d^{2}(F^{a})

F
. For instance,

and now the two right hand sides agree since

. The incubator
