4.14.
Substitution of nullary into ternary:

Consider a loose ternary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
and three nullary maps
a\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{A}
,
b\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{B}
and
c\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{C}
. We define
F\circ_{1}a:=F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
,
F\circ_{2}b:=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
and
F\circ_{3}c=F_{c}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{D}
.

By definition of tight ternary maps, if
F
is tight, so are
F\circ_{2}b
and
F\circ_{3}c
, as required.

Naturality of the above three substitutions follow from the description of substitution of ternary and unary in Table
5
.
All of the cases are similar. For example, consider
b\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
together with
Q
and
F
as in Table
5
. Then

(F\circ_{2}Q)\circ_{2}b:=(F\circ_{2}Q)\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}:=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle Qb$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle Qb$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle Qb$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle Qb$}}}
whilst similarly
F\circ_{2}(Q\circ_{1}b):=F\circ_{2}Qb:=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle Qb$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle Qb$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle Qb$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle Qb$}}}
.

By analogy with Lemma
4.5
, we have the following trivial result relating
\lambda_{3}
with
\lambda_{2}
in the context of a nullary map. As in Lemma
4.5
, the proof is simply a matter of tracing through the definitions.

Lemma 4.8
.

Given a nullary map
a_{i}\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{A}_{i}
and binary map
F\colon\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
we have an equality of binary maps
\lambda_{2}(F\circ_{i}a)=\lambda_{3}(F)\circ_{i}a
.

4.15.
Substitution of binary into binary

First variable

Given
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{X}
and
G\colon\mathcal{X},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
we define the substitution

G\circ_{1}F:=\lambda_{3}({\lambda_{2}}^{-1}(G)\circ_{1}F)

where
{\lambda_{2}}^{-1}(G)\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
is the adjoint map. Naturality of this substitution follows from the naturality of the components
\lambda_{3}
,
\lambda_{2}
and
\circ_{1}
(for binary and unary maps) involved in its construction.

Observe also that if
F
and
G
are tight, then since
\lambda_{2}
respects tightness, the binary map
\lambda_{2}^{-1}(G)
is tight. Therefore so is the composite
\lambda_{2}^{-1}(G)\circ_{1}F
, and since
\lambda_{3}
also respects tightness, we have that
G\circ_{1}F
is tight, as required.

Second variable

Consider
F\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{X}
and
G\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{D}
. Firstly, we use the duality bijection
d^{2}
to form

d^{2}G\colon\mathcal{X}^{co},\mathcal{A}^{co}\to\mathcal{D}^{co}\hskip 14.22636pt\textnormal{and}\hskip 14.22636ptd^{2}F\colon\mathcal{C}^{co},\mathcal{B}^{co}\to\mathcal{X}^{co}.

Then, we form
d^{2}G\circ_{1}d^{2}F\colon\mathcal{C}^{co},\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{A}^{co}\to\mathcal{D}^{co}
before dualising again to define

G\circ_{2}F:=d^{3}(d^{2}G\circ_{1}d^{2}F)\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}.

It follows from naturality of
d^{2}
,
d^{3}
and
\circ_{1}
for binary maps that
\circ_{2}
is natural in each variable.

6
below describes the substitutions of binary into binary.

Suppose that

is tight, which is to say that

4.16.
A
3
-ary skew multicategory

We have defined all of the structure for the
3
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
and verified all associativity equations, except those relating nullary maps with the two above substitutions
\circ_{1}
and
\circ_{2}
of binary into binary. In each case there are three equations, and all six follow directly from the description in Table
6
.

4.17.
4-ary maps

A
loose 4-ary map

F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
consists of:

•

at
a\in\mathcal{A}
, a loose ternary map
F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
;

•

at
b\in\mathcal{B}
, a loose ternary map
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
;

•

at
c\in\mathcal{C}
, a loose ternary map
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
;

•

at
d\in\mathcal{D}
, a loose ternary map
F_{d}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}
;

such that the following six equations between loose binary maps hold

F^{a}(b,-,-)=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(a,-,-)=:F^{a}_{b}\quad F^{a}(-,c,-)=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}(a,-,-)=:F^{a}_{c}

F^{a}(-,-,d)=F_{d}(a,-,-)=:F^{a}_{d}\quad F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(-,c,-)=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}(-,b,-)=:F^{b}_{c}

F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(-,-,d)=F_{d}(-,b,-)=:F^{b}_{d}\quad F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}(-,-,d)=F_{d}(-,-,c)=:F^{c}_{d}

and such that the
mecon axiom
is satisfied (see Equation (
Mcn
) in
Section

D.3
).

A loose
4
-ary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
is tight if the ternary maps
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
,
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
and
F_{d}
are tight for all
b\in\mathcal{B},c\in\mathcal{C}
and
d\in\mathcal{D}
.

Remark 4.9
.

There is some redundancy in the above definition of tight
4
-ary maps. In fact, any two of
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
,
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
and
F_{d}
being tight implies the third is tight. Indeed if
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
are
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
tight, consider
F_{d}
: we must show that
F_{d}(b,-,-)
and
F_{d}(-,c,-)
are tight binary maps, but these equal
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}(-,-,d)
and
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}(-,-,d)
which are tight by assumption.

4.18.
The correspondence between
4
-ary and
3
-ary maps

Proposition 4.10
.

There is a bijection

\lambda_{4}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{3}(\,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})\,)\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D};\mathcal{E}),

which restricts to tight maps on either side.

Proof.

Consider a ternary map
\overline{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})
. This is specified by:

(1)

three binary maps
\overline{F}^{a}\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})
,
\overline{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})
and
\overline{F}_{c}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})
;

(2)

a perturbation
(A|B|C)
in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})
;

all satisfying the ternary map equations. Now, we will describe the associated
4
-ary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
. It is convenient, for fixed objects
a,b,c,d
to consider the diagram below.

Firstly, the three ternary maps
\overline{F}^{a}=\overline{F}\circ_{1}a
,
\overline{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}=\overline{F}\circ_{2}b
and
\overline{F}_{c}=\overline{F}\circ_{3}c
correspond under the bijection
\lambda_{3}
of Proposition
4.6
to
F^{a}\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E},F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
and
F_{c}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
. Also, for each
d\in\mathcal{D}
we have the composite ternary map
F_{d}:=ev_{d}\circ_{1}F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})\to\mathcal{E}
.

We must establish the six equations relating the four ternary maps, which are parametrised by a choice of two elements from
\{a,b,c,d\}
. Each of these corresponds to one of the six associativity equations visible in the above diagram, involving the ternary map and any two of the other four multimaps (nullary or unary). The argument here is identical in form to the corresponding part of the proof of Proposition
4.6
, but using Lemma
4.8
instead of Lemma
4.5
, and we leave the details to the reader.

The perturbation axiom for
(A|B|C)
is precisely the mecon axiom.

Finally,
\overline{F}
is tight just when
\overline{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
and
\overline{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
are tight, but since
\lambda_{3}
respects tightness, this is precisely to say that
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
and
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
are tight. By Remark
4.9
, these two conditions fully capture tightness of
4
-maps — that is, tightness of
F_{d}
follows automatically.
∎

4.19.
The functor of
4
-ary maps

Consider again the bijection

\lambda_{4}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{3}(\,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})\,)\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D};\mathcal{E}).

As in the cases of
\lambda_{2}
and
\lambda_{3}
, the right hand side admits the unique structure of a functor

\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(-;-)\colon(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{op})^{4}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{Set}

such that
\lambda_{4}
becomes natural in each variable. This defines the substitution of
4
-ary and unary maps.

Furthermore, the behaviour of
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)
, as per Proposition
3.6
, ensures that
F\circ_{1}P
is tight if
F
and
P
are,
F\circ_{i}P
is always tight if
F
is and
i>1
, and
Q\circ_{1}F
is tight if both
Q
and
F
are, where
F
is a 4-ary map and
P
and
Q
unary.

In
Table

7
below, we spell out the details of substitution of
4
-ary and unary.

4.20.
The duality isomorphism in dimension
4

Proposition 4.11
.

There is a bijection

d^{3}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D};\mathcal{E})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}};\mathcal{E}^{\mathit{co}}),

natural in each variable.

Proof.

Given
F\in\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D};\mathcal{E})
, we define
d^{4}F\in\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}};\mathcal{D}^{\mathit{co}})
.

We set

d^{4}F^{d}:=d^{3}(F_{d}),d^{4}F^{d}:=d^{3}(F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}),d^{4}F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}:=d^{3}(F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}})\textnormal{ and }d^{4}F_{a}:=d^{3}(F^{a}).

The six equations concerning the interaction of these ternary maps follow from the corresponding equations for
F
. For instance,

(d^{4}F^{d})(-,-,a):=d^{3}(F_{d})_{a}:=d^{2}(F_{d}(a-,-))

whilst

(d^{4}F_{a})(d,-,-):=d^{3}(F^{a})^{d}:=d^{2}(F^{a}(-,-,d))

and now the two right hand sides agree since
(F_{d})(a,-,-)=(F^{a})(-,-,d)
. The mecon axiom for
F
, which involves the equality of two
3
-cells in
\mathcal{D}
, coincides with the mecon axiom for
d^{4}F
viewing these
3
-cells as belonging to
\mathcal{D}^{\mathit{co}}
by reversing the orientations of their bounding
2
-cells.

Naturality of
d^{4}
follows from naturality of
d^{3}
and to see that
d^{4}
is a natural bijection, simply observe that

d^{4}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D};\mathcal{E})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{4}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}};\mathcal{E}^{\mathit{co}})
has
d^{4}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{B}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathit{co}},\mathcal{E}^{\mathit{co}}}
as its inverse.
∎

4.21.
Substitution of nullary into
4
-ary

Consider a loose
4
-ary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
and four nullary maps
a\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{A}
,
b\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{B}
,
c\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{C}
and
d\colon\diamond\to\mathcal{D}
. We define
F\circ_{1}a:=F^{a}
,
F\circ_{2}b:=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
,
F\circ_{3}c=F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
and
F\circ_{4}d=F_{d}
.

If
F
is tight, so are
F\circ_{2}b
,
F\circ_{3}c
and
F\circ_{4}d
by definition of these substitutions.

The six associativity equations involving two nullary maps and a
4
-ary map reduce to the six equalities of binary maps in the definition of a
4
-ary map. As before, naturality of the four substitutions of nullary into

4
-ary and unary in Table

4.22.
Substitution of ternary into binary

First variable

Given
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{X}
and
G\colon\mathcal{X},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
we define the substitution

G\circ_{1}F:=\lambda_{4}({\lambda_{2}}^{-1}(G)\circ_{1}F)

where
{\lambda_{2}}^{-1}(G)\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})
is the adjoint map.

Naturality of this substitution follows from naturality of
\lambda_{4}
,
\lambda_{2}
and the substitution
\circ_{1}
of ternary maps.

The multimap
G\circ_{1}F
is tight whenever
F
and
G
are. Indeed, if
G
is tight, then as
\lambda_{2}
respects tightness, so is
(\lambda_{2})^{-1}(G)
. Therefore as
\circ_{1}
for binary maps respects tightness,
(\lambda_{2})^{-1}(G)\circ_{1}F
is tight. Finally, since
\lambda_{4}
respects tightness,
G\circ_{1}F
is tight.

Consider

and

Then, we form
d^{2}G\circ_{1}d^{2}F\colon\mathcal{D}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co},\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{A}^{co}\to\mathcal{E}^{co}
before dualising again using
d^{4}
to define

G\circ_{2}F:=d^{4}(d^{2}G\circ_{1}d^{3}F)\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}.

It follows from naturality of

d^{4}
and naturality of

\circ_{2}
is natural in each variable.

4.24.
A
4
-ary skew multicategory

We have defined all of the structure for the
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
and verified all associativity equations except those involving (1) a binary map, a ternary map and a nullary map or (2) three binary maps. The first group of associativity equations follow directly from the definitions of substitution of ternary and binary given in Tables
8
and
9
.

It remains to consider the second group of equations involving three binary maps. In fact, given that
4
-ary maps are determined by their four ternary components, the remaining equations follow easily from what we have already done. For a representative example, consider

F\colon\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{X}
,
G\colon\mathcal{X},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{Y}
and
H\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{E}
.

F
\mathcal{B}
\mathcal{C}
G
\mathcal{X}
\mathcal{D}
H
\mathcal{A}
\mathcal{Y}
\mathcal{E}

We must prove that
(H\circ_{2}G)\circ_{2}F=H\circ_{2}(G\circ_{1}F)
. To prove these
4
-ary maps are equal, we must show that their four defining ternary maps are the same.
We have

((H\circ_{2}G)\circ_{2}F)^{a}=(H\circ_{2}G)^{a}\circ_{2}F=(H^{a}\circ_{1}G)\circ_{2}F

and similarly

H\circ_{2}(G\circ_{1}F)^{a}=H^{a}\circ_{1}(G\circ_{1}F)

where all equalities follow from the explicit descriptions of substitutions given in Tables
6
,
8
and
9
. The equality of the right hand sides is just naturality of
\circ_{2}
in unary maps.

Similarly, the necessary equalities in
b,c
and
d
reduce to the associativity equations

(H\circ_{2}G)\circ_{1}F^{b}=H\circ_{2}(G\circ_{1}F^{b})
,
(H\circ_{2}G)\circ_{1}F_{c}=H\circ_{2}(G\circ_{1}F_{c})
and
(H\circ_{2}G_{d})\circ_{2}F=H\circ_{2}(G_{d}\circ_{1}F)

all of which are just instances of naturality in unary maps, which hold in the
3
-multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
.

Putting the results of this section together, we have proven:

Theorem 4.12
.

With the structure described in this section,
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
forms a
4
-ary skew multicategory.

5.
The skew monoidal closed structure capturing lax transformations

In this section we will use the
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
of Section
4
to construct the closed skew monoidal category
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{l},1)
with internal hom
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. In order to do this, we must start by establishing further properties of
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
— firstly, we establish closedness and then left representability. Combining these results, in
Theorem

5.8
we obtain the skew monoidal structure of
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{l},1)
.

5.1.
Closedness

To this end, recall the natural bijection
\lambda_{2}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{l}(\mathcal{A};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
of Section
4.4
and Section
4.6
which restricts to tight maps on either side. Its unit is a binary map

ev=\lambda_{2}(1_{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})})\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}

whose universal property is that given a binary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
there exists a unique unary map
\overline{F}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
such that
ev\circ_{1}\overline{F}=F
. Note that
ev\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
is
tight
, since it corresponds to the identity on
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
which is tight.

Theorem 5.1
.

The tight binary maps
ev\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
exhibit
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
as a closed
4
-ary skew multicategory.

Proof.

Consider the bijections

\lambda_{n+1}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{n}^{l}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{n+1}^{l}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})

of
Section

4
. We have constructed these for
n=0,1,2
and
3
and shown that, for
n>0
, these restrict to bijections on tight maps. What remains to show, in each case, is that
\lambda_{n+1}(F)=ev\circ_{1}F
.

Firstly, consider
\lambda_{1}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{0}^{l}(\diamond;\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{l}(\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
and
F\colon\diamond\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
. Then

\lambda_{1}(F)=\lambda_{1}(1_{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})}\circ_{1}F)=\lambda_{2}(1_{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})})\circ_{1}F=ev\circ_{1}F

where the first equality holds by functoriality, the second by Lemma
4.5
and the third by definition of
ev
.

For
\lambda_{2}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{l}(\mathcal{A};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{l}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
we have that
\lambda_{2}(F)=ev\circ_{1}F
by definition of
ev
as the unit of the natural bijection.

Next, consider
\lambda_{3}\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{2}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{3}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})
. We have

\lambda_{3}(F)=\lambda_{3}(1_{\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})}\circ_{1}F)=\lambda_{3}({\lambda_{2}}^{-1}(ev)\circ_{1}F)=ev\circ_{1}F

where
the first equality holds by functoriality, the second by definition of
ev_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}}
and the third by definition of
\circ_{1}
for binary maps. The case of
\lambda_{4}
is identical in form to that of
\lambda_{3}
.

∎

If we forget the skew aspects, we have a still stronger result.

Theorem 5.2
.

The underlying
4
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}
of loose multimaps is biclosed, with right internal hom
\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
.

Proof.

Given the natural isomorphism
(-)^{+}_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathbf{Oplax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co})^{co}
, the problem is equally to prove the corresponding result for the homs
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co})^{co}
. To this end, we observe that applying the duality
d^{2}
to
ev\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co}),\mathcal{B}^{co}\to\mathcal{C}^{co}
give rise to a binary map

e:=d^{2}(ev)\colon\mathcal{B},\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co})^{co}\to\mathcal{C}

and we will show that the induced function

e\circ_{2}-\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{n}^{l}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B}^{co},\mathcal{C}^{co})^{co})\cong\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{n+1}^{l}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathcal{C})

is a bijection for
n=0,1,2,3
. In fact the cases
n=2,3
are easiest. For
n=2
and a binary map
F
, we have

e\circ_{2}F:=d^{3}(d^{2}e\circ_{1}d^{2}F)=d^{3}(ev\circ_{1}d^{2}F).

In particular,
e\circ_{2}-
is the composite of three bijections
d^{2}
,
ev\circ_{1}-
and
d^{3}
and so a bijection too. The case
n=3
is identical in form since substitution of ternary maps into binary maps is defined using duality and
\circ_{1}
in the same way.

For
n=1
,
e\circ_{2}F:=d^{2}(ev)\circ_{2}F=d^{2}(ev\circ_{1}F^{co})
where the second equality holds by naturality of
d^{2}
. In particular,
e\circ_{2}-
is again a composite of three bijections
d^{2}
,
ev\circ_{1}-
and
(-)^{co}
and so a bijection.

For
n=0
, observe that for a nullary map
x
(viewed as an object of its codomain) we have
e\circ_{2}x:=d^{2}(ev)\circ_{2}x=d^{2}(ev)_{x}=(ev)^{x}=(ev)\circ_{1}x
where the second equality is by definition of
d^{2}
. Hence,
e\circ_{2}-
is a bijection since
ev\circ_{1}-
is such on nullary maps.
∎

5.2.
Left representability

Following Section
2.5
, to show that
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}
is left representable, we must show that it has a nullary map classifier and tight binary map classifiers.

Let us first deal with the nullary map classifier, which is simply the terminal Gray-category
\mathbf{1}
.

Proposition 5.3
.

The
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
has nullary map classifier
u\colon\diamond\to\mathbf{1}
, where
u
is the nullary map selecting the single object
\bullet
of the terminal Gray-category
\mathbf{1}
.

Proof.

The function
-\circ_{1}u\colon\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{t}_{1}(\mathbf{1};\mathcal{A})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})
sends
F\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{A}
to its value at
\bullet
— this function is clearly a bijection.
∎

Remark 5.4
.

In fact,
u\colon\diamond\to\mathbf{1}
is also a nullary map classifier in the
4
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}
of loose multimaps, since, because of the normality conditions for a pseudomap, every pseudomap out of
\mathbf{1}
is strict.

The tight binary map classifiers
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{B}
can be shown to exist in two ways. Following Section
2.5
, the first approach is to show each
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)
has a left adjoint, which can be done by appealing to an adjoint functor theorem. This approach emphasises that the skew monoidal structure can be constructed without requiring any explicit description of the tensor product
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{B}
. The second approach is to construct
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{B}
using a
presentation
. We describe both approaches here, beginning with the first. The reader more interested in the approach via presentations may skip directly to Section
5.3
.

In order to prove that each
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)
has a left adjoint, it will be helpful to first consider Gohla’s construction of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
using his
path space
functor.

Remark 5.5
.

Gohla’s construction of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
in Section 5 of
[
20
]
begins with the construction of a path space functor
P\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
, which comes equipped with natural transformations
i\colon 1\to P
and
s,t\colon P\rightrightarrows 1
satisfying
s\circ i=t\circ i=1
. In fact
P=\mathbf{Lax}(\mathbf{2},-)
and his construction of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
builds on this. We can look at his construction more abstractly as follows.

A
path object functor
on a category
\mathcal{C}
can be defined as a functor
P\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
equipped with natural transformations
i\colon 1\to P
and
s,t\colon P\to 1
satisfying
s\circ i=1=t\circ i
. This defines a functor
P\colon\mathcal{C}\to[\mathbb{G}_{1}^{op},\mathcal{C}]
to the category of reflexive graphs in
\mathcal{C}
and, if
\mathcal{C}
has finite limits, it can be extended inductively to a functor
P_{\bullet}\colon\mathcal{C}\to[\mathbb{G}_{n}^{op},\mathcal{C}]
, the category of reflexive
n
-graphs in
\mathcal{C}
. Here
P_{n+2}\mathcal{A}
is defined as the pullback in the square left below.

(13)

\textstyle{P_{n+2}\mathcal{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\langle s_{n+1},t_{n+1}\rangle}
\textstyle{P(P_{n+1}\mathcal{A})^{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{Ps_{n}\times Pt_{n}}
\scriptstyle{s\times t}
\textstyle{(P_{n+1}\mathcal{A})^{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{s_{n}\times t_{n}}
\textstyle{(P_{n}\mathcal{A})^{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{i\times i}
\textstyle{P(P_{n}\mathcal{A})^{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{s\times t}
\textstyle{(P_{n}\mathcal{A})^{2}}

The maps
s_{n+1}
and
t_{n+1}
are obtained as the composite on the top row, as depicted, and the globularity relations follow by chasing the above diagram under post-composition with the two product projections. The reflexivity map
i_{n+1}\colon P_{n+1}\mathcal{A}\to P_{n+2}\mathcal{A}
is the unique map to the pullback induced by
\langle i,i\rangle\colon P_{n+1}\mathcal{A}\to P(P_{n+1}\mathcal{A})^{2}
and
\langle s_{n+1},t_{n+1}\rangle\colon P_{n+1}\mathcal{A}\to(P_{n}\mathcal{A})^{2}
.

Doing this, Gohla produces a functor
P_{\bullet}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to[\mathbb{G}_{3}^{op},\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}]
and shows, in fact, that each
3
-globular object
P_{\bullet}\mathcal{B}
underlies an
internal Gray-category
in
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
— here, the pseudomaps are essential. Accordingly, given a Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
, the hom globular set
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}(\mathcal{A},P_{\bullet}\mathcal{B})
underlies a Gray-category. This is exactly
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
— in particular, the
n
-cells are
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
correspond to pseudomaps
\mathcal{A}\to P_{n}\mathcal{B}
.

Proposition 5.6
.

For each Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
, the functor
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
has a left adjoint.

Proof.

Our proof will use that the category
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is locally finitely presentable (l.f.p.) because such categories permit an easily verifiable adjoint functor theorem. Namely a functor between l.f.p. categories has a left adjoint just when it preserves limits and is accessible (that is, preserves
\lambda
-filtered colimits for some regular cardinal
\lambda
). This is Theorem 1.66 of
[
1
]
, to which we also refer the reader as a reference on l.f.p. categories.

To show that
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is l.f.p, we use Theorem 4.5 of
[
28
]
, which asserts that if the monoidal biclosed category
\mathcal{V}
is l.f.p., then
\mathcal{V}
-
\mathbf{Cat}
is too. Starting with the cartesian closed l.f.p. category of sets this establishes that
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is l.f.p. in two further steps, passing through the cartesian closed category of categories, followed by the Gray-tensor product of
2
-categories.

Given the above, it remains to prove that each
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
preserves limits and is accessible. Since a Gray-functor is invertible just when its underlying morphism of
3
-graphs is, it follows that
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
has strong generator
\{D_{i}:i=0,1,2,3\}
where
D_{i}
denotes the free
i
-cell. Since each
D_{i}
is a finitely presentable (indeed, finite) Gray-category, the representable
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(D_{i},-)
preserves limits and filtered colimits. Being jointly conservative, they also reflect limits and filtered colimits. Therefore
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)
will preserve limits and be accessible just when each composite
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(D_{i},\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-))
has these properties. But following Remark
5.5
, we have a natural isomorphism

\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(D_{i},\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-))\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}(A,P_{i}(-))\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(QA,P_{i}(-))=\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(QA,-)\circ P_{i}.

By Examples 2.17(1) of
[
1
]
, each representable preserves limits and is accessible. Therefore it suffices to prove that each
P_{i}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
has these properties — we will prove that each preserves limits and all filtered colimits.

Certainly, this is true for the identity functor
P_{0}
and let us suppose that we can prove it for
P_{1}=P
. Then by the left pullback square in Equation (
13
), we will obtain
P_{2}
and
P_{3}
inductively as finite limits of functors, each of which preserve limits and filtered colimits. Since finite limits commute with limits (in any category) and filtered colimits (in any l.f.p. one) it will follow that
P_{2}
and
P_{3}
has these preservation properties too. Therefore it remains to prove that
P
preserves limits and filtered colimits.

Arguing as before, we must prove that
P(-)_{i}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{Set}
has these properties for
i=0,1,2,3
. In fact each of these functors is represented by a finite, and so finitely presentable, Gray-category. Now the elements of
P(\mathcal{A})_{0}
are the
1
-cells in
\mathcal{A}
— in particular, we have a natural isomorphism
P(\mathcal{A})_{0}\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(D_{1},\mathcal{A})
. The elements of
P(\mathcal{A})_{1}
are the lax squares, or
1
-cylinders, in
\mathcal{A}
. Hence we have a natural isomorphism
P(\mathcal{A})_{1}\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(C_{1},\mathcal{A})
, where
C_{1}
is the free lax square drawn below.

\textstyle{0}
\textstyle{1}
\textstyle{2}
\textstyle{3}

The elements of
P(\mathcal{A})_{2}
and
P(\mathcal{A})_{3}
are
2
- and
3
-cylinders, as described in detail in
[
20
, Definition 3.1]
, and are represented by the free
2
/
3
-cylinders. Whilst, we omit writing them down here, we note that they are both finite
3
-categories (no horizontally composable
2
-cells arise) whose descriptions can easily be extracted from
[
20
, Definition 3.1]
.

∎

In particular, putting the above results together, we have:

Theorem 5.7
.

The
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
is left representable and closed, with internal hom
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

5.3.
A presentation of the Gray-category
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{B}

Let us begin by defining
presentations of Gray-categories.
Informally, firstly, a presentation of a Gray-category
\mathcal{A}
consists of

(1)

a set
X_{0}
of
0
-cells;

(2)

a set
X_{1}
of
1
-cells with specified source and target in
X_{0}
;

(3)

a set

(that is, parallel

\mathcal{A}_{1}

and

(4)

of
3

The

\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
is locally presentable and therefore cocomplete.

Now for

-cells. (Here we set

for the codiagonal.

Formally, a presentation of
\mathcal{A}

as on the left below

(14)

\textstyle{X_{i}.B_{i-1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

The morphism

The morphism

of

Now let

5.4.
The closed skew monoidal structure

Given Theorem
5.7
, the construction of Section
2.6
immediately yields:

Theorem 5.8
.

There is a closed skew monoidal structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{l},\mathbf{1})
whose internal hom is
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

Let us describe the skew monoidal structure in a little more detail and explore some of its properties.

•

The tensor product
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{B}
is the tight binary map classifier, and the unit is the terminal Gray-category
\mathbf{1}
.

•

The left unit map
l_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
is, as described in Section
2.6
, the counit of the adjunction with right adjoint the inclusion
j\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
of tight unary into loose unary. Accordingly, this is the counit
p_{\mathcal{A}}\colon Q\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
of the pseudomorphism classifier comonad of Remark
3.1
. Since the counit
p_{\mathcal{A}}
is a triequivalence, we conclude that
l_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
is a triequivalence for all
\mathcal{A}
.

•

By construction, the right unit map
r_{\mathcal{A}}
is given by
\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathbf{1}}\circ_{2}u\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathbf{1}
. We will show that
r_{\mathcal{A}}
is invertible, so that the skew monoidal structure is right normal. Indeed, by Yoneda, this is equivalent to show that the composite

\textstyle{\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{t}(\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathbf{1};\mathcal{B})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{-\circ\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathbf{1}}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{2}^{t}(\mathcal{A},\mathbf{1};\mathcal{B})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{-\circ_{2}u}
\textstyle{\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}_{1}^{t}(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{B})}

is invertible. Since its first component is so, we must show that
-\circ_{2}u

is invertible. But this is clearly the case, since a tight binary map
\mathcal{A},\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{B}
just amounts to a strict map
\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
.

•

Let us show that the associator is not, in general, invertible. One of the axioms for a skew monoidal category gives the commutative diagram below.

\textstyle{(\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}\mathbf{1})\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1},\mathcal{A}}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}(\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}l_{\mathcal{A}}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{r_{\mathbf{1}}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A}}
\scriptstyle{1}
\textstyle{\mathbf{1}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{A}}

Since the left vertical is invertible the
\alpha_{\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1},\mathcal{A}}
is invertible just when the right vertical is. This is
Qp_{\mathcal{A}}\colon Q^{2}\mathcal{A}\to Q\mathcal{A}
. So, as long as
\mathcal{A}
has a composable pair of non-identity maps
f\colon x\to y
and
g\colon y\to z
,
Qp
will identify the parallel pair
[[gf]],\,[[g],[f]]\colon x\rightrightarrows z\in Q^{2}\mathcal{A}
, and hence fail to be invertible. In particular, the associator is not in general invertible.

6.
The skew monoidal closed structure capturing pseudo-transformations

In this section, we introduce the notion of
pseudo-transformation
and the Gray-category of pseudo-transformations
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. We then describe a closed
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}
of
pseudo-multimaps
with internal hom
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. Using this, we construct in Theorem
6.3
a closed skew monoidal structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},\mathbf{1})
with internal hom
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

Both pseudo-transformations and pseudo-binary maps enhance their lax counterparts by equipping them with certain adjoint equivalences. As such, let us begin by fixing a little notation concerning adjoint equivalences in
2
-categories.

6.1.
Adjoint equivalences in
2
-categories

Let
\mathcal{K}
be a
2
-category. The category
\mathbf{AE}(\mathcal{K})
of adjoint equivalences in
\mathcal{K}
has the same objects as
\mathcal{K}
whilst a morphism
(\epsilon,f\dashv g,\eta)\colon x\to y
is an adjoint equivalence
(\epsilon,f\dashv g,\eta)
with
g\colon x\to y
the right adjoint.

•

Given adjoint equivalences
(\epsilon,f\dashv g,\eta)\colon x\to y
and
(\epsilon^{\prime},f^{\prime}\dashv g^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})\colon y\to z
the composite adjoint equivalence is given by
(\epsilon\cdot f\epsilon^{\prime}g,\,ff^{\prime}\dashv g^{\prime}g,\,g^{\prime}\eta f^{\prime}\cdot\eta^{\prime})\colon x\to z
.

•

For
x\in\mathcal{K}
, the identity adjoint equivalence is
1_{x}\dashv 1_{x}\colon x\to x
.

A 2-functor
F\colon\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{L}
induces a functor
\mathbf{AE}(F)\colon\mathbf{AE}(\mathcal{K})\to\mathbf{AE}(\mathcal{L})
sending
f\dashv g\colon x\to y
to
Ff\dashv Fg\colon Fx\to Fy
.

6.2.
The Gray-category of pseudo-transformations

Let us now define the Gray-category
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
of pseudo-transformations between two Gray-categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
. Its cells are defined as follows.

•

0-cells:
pseudomaps
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
.

•

1-cells:
pseudo-transformations — these are lax transformations
\alpha\colon F\to G
equipped with, for any 1-cell
f\colon x\to y\in\mathcal{A}
, an adjoint equivalence
\alpha^{o}_{f}\dashv\alpha_{f}\colon Gf\alpha_{x}\to\alpha_{y}Ff
such that:

(a)

at an object
x\in\mathcal{A}
,
\alpha^{o}_{1_{x}}\dashv\alpha_{1_{x}}
is the identity adjoint equivalence;

(b)

at a
2
-cell
\phi\colon f\to f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
, the 3-cell
\alpha_{\phi}
is invertible.

•

2-cells:
pseudo-modifications — these are modifications
\Lambda\colon\alpha\to\beta
such that, for any 1-cell
f\colon x\to y\in\mathcal{A}
, the 3-cell
\Lambda_{f}
is invertible.

•

3-cells:
perturbations
\theta\colon\Lambda\to\Gamma
.

Remark 6.1
.

The notation
\alpha^{o}_{f}
for the left adjoint of the adjoint equivalence is intended to suggest that
\alpha^{o}_{f}
is the component of an
oplax transformation
. This hints at a more symmetric presentation of the notion of pseudo-transformation, which we will explore further in a followup paper.

Our aim is now to equip
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
with the structure of a Gray-category such that the forgetful
3
-graph map
U\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
becomes a strict Gray-functor.

The identity
1\colon F\to F
pseudo-transformation is given by the identity in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
equipped with the identity adjoint equivalences in each component. Given a composable pair
\alpha\colon F\to G
and
\beta\colon G\to H
of pseudo-transformations, their composite
\beta\alpha\colon F\to H
in
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
is given by their composite in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
equipped with

•

at
f\colon x\to y\in\mathcal{A}
, the composite adjoint equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Hf\beta_{x}\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\beta_{y}Gf\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\beta_{y}\alpha_{y}Ff.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{f}\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta^{o}_{f}\circ 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\top}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ\alpha_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\circ\alpha^{o}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\top}

To see that
\beta\alpha
is in fact a pseudo-transformation, firstly suppose that
f
is an identity
1
-cell. As
\alpha
and
\beta
are pseudo-transformations,
\beta^{o}_{f}\dashv\beta_{f}
and
\alpha^{o}_{f}\dashv\alpha_{f}
are identity adjoint equivalences. Applying the whiskering
2
-functors
-\circ\alpha_{x}
and
\beta_{y}\circ-
produces identity adjoint equivalences, the two components depicted above, whose composite is therefore the identity adjoint equivalence too, as required. Furthermore, the
3
-cell
(\beta\alpha)_{\phi}
is invertible since, as described explicitly in Equation (
17
) of
Appendix

B
, it is a composite of whiskers of the invertible 3-cells
\beta_{\phi}
and
\alpha_{\phi}
.

Associativity of
1
-cell composition in
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
follows from associativity in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, associativity of composition of adjoint equivalences in a
2
-category plus
2
-functoriality of whiskering by
1
-cells. The unital laws easily follow, hence we get a category structure on
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
making
U
a functor. With regards
2
-cells, we must show that pseudo-modifications are closed in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
under vertical composition, whiskering by pseudomaps and identities. In each case, we simply need to show that the
3
-cell components of the relevant modifications in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
are invertible — this follows directly from the descriptions of these operations on modifications in
Appendix

B
. Since
3
-cells in
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
are just perturbations, we define their composites and the interchange maps just as in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
. This establishes that
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
is a Gray-category and
U\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
a strict Gray-functor.

Next, let
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
G\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
be pseudo-functors between Gray-categories. Lifting the action of
\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)
and using that
F
and
G
are locally 2-functors (and hence preserve local adjoint equivalences), we obtain:

•

A strict map
\mathbf{Psd}(F,\mathcal{B})\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

•

A pseudomap
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},G)\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
which is strict if
G
is.

Both
\mathbf{Psd}(F,\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},G)
act on
0
-cells, that is pseudomaps, by composition. Consider a pseudo-transformation
\beta\colon G\to G^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B})
. Then
\mathbf{Psd}(F,\mathcal{B})(\beta)
is the lax transformation
\beta F
equipped with, at
f\colon x\to y\in\mathcal{A}
, the adjoint equivalence
\beta^{o}_{Ff}\dashv\beta_{Ff}
. Given
\alpha\colon F\to F^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, the pseudo-transformation
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},G)(\alpha)
is the lax transformation
G\alpha
equipped with, for
f\colon x\to y\in\mathcal{A}
, the composite adjoint equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{GF^{\prime}fG\alpha_{x}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G(F^{\prime}f\alpha_{x})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G(\alpha_{y}Ff)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G\alpha_{y}GFf}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(G^{2})^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(\alpha_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G({\alpha^{o}_{f}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G^{2}}^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\top}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\top}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\top}

in which the isomorphisms and their inverses, on the left and the right, are viewed as adjoint equivalences with identity counit and unit.

The higher-dimensional structure of
\mathbf{Psd}(F,\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},G)
is exactly as for
\mathbf{Lax}(F,\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},G)
. With this description, we obtain a Gray-functor
\mathbf{Psd}(-,-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}
and natural transformation
U\colon\mathbf{Psd}(-,-)\to\mathbf{Lax}(-,-)
. We leave to the reader the routine verifications of naturality, which, again, amount to checking the equality of a few adjoint equivalences.

6.3.
The
4
-ary skew multicategory of Gray-categories and pseudo-multimaps

We will construct the set of
n
-ary pseudo-multimaps inductively, together with a forgetful function

\mathbb{U}_{n}\colon\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B})
, and will sometimes refer to the elements of

as

multimaps.

Nullary pseudo-multimaps are just objects as before; that is, we have

\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A}):=\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})

with
\mathbb{U}_{0}
the identity function. For higher

, they are defined via the pullback

(15)

\textstyle{\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n+1}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbb{U}_{n+1}}
\scriptstyle{(\lambda_{n+1}^{p})^{-1}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\,\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\,)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(U_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\circ_{1}-)\circ\mathbb{U}_{n}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{n+1}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\lambda_{n+1})^{-1}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{n}(\,\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\,)}

where the lower horizontal is the inverse of the closedness bijection for lax multimaps constructed in
Section

Unpacking the above yields the following descriptions:

•

A pseudo unary map
\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
is just a pseudomap
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
.

•

A pseudo binary map
\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
consists of a lax binary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
in
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}
equipped with adjoint equivalences

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F^{a^{\prime}}_{B}F^{A}_{b}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F^{A}_{b^{\prime}}F^{a}_{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A^{o}_{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\top}

in
\mathcal{C}(F^{a}_{b},F^{a^{\prime}}_{b^{\prime}})
such that:

(i)

given objects

and

, the adjoint equivalences
{A^{o}_{1_{b}}}\dashv A_{1_{b}}
and
{{(1_{a})}^{o}_{B}}\dashv{(1_{a})}_{B}
are identities;

(ii)

given 1-cells
A\in\mathcal{A}
and
B\in\mathcal{B}
and 2-cells

and

, the

and

in
\mathcal{C}
are invertible.

•

A pseudo ternary map

\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
with invertible incubators
(A\mid B\mid C)
together with pseudo-binary maps
\mathbf{F}^{a}
,
\mathbf{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
and
\mathbf{F}_{c}
whose underlying lax binary maps are
{F}^{a}
,
{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
and
{F}_{c}

•

A pseudo 4-ary map
\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
consists of a lax 4-ary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
together with pseudo-ternary maps
\mathbf{F}^{a}
,
\mathbf{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
,
\mathbf{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
and

satisfying the six compatibility equations of Section

(but with

substituted for

) and whose underlying lax ternary maps are
F^{a}
,
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
,
F\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
and

.

When
n=0
, the sets
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})
form a functor
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}
for which the (identity) components
\mathbb{U}_{0}\colon\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{0}(\diamond;\mathcal{A})
are natural in
\mathcal{A}
. Using the established naturality of

, by induction the sets

obtain the unique structure of a functor
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(-;-)\colon(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}^{n})^{op}\times\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}\to\mathbf{Set}
for which the pullback projections in (
15
) are natural in each variable. Replacing the horizontal bijections in the pullback square by their inverses, this is equally to say that the pullback projections in

(16)

\textstyle{\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\,\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\,)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(U_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\circ_{1}-)\circ\mathbb{U}_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{n+1}^{p}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n+1}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}_{n}(\,\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\,)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

are natural.

Now that we have the

4
-ary multicategory.
Let us split them into two groups. All are straightforward enhancements of the lax case — none involve checking any equations between adjoint equivalences, but only verifying that some
3
-cells are invertible.

•

Firstly, we consider substitutions involving nullary maps. Given

, we define

and
\mathbf{F}\circ_{2}b=F_{b}
, noting that unary maps are the same in the lax and pseudo-cases. Given
\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}

,
\mathbf{F}\circ_{2}b=\mathbf{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}

\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}

\mathbf{F}\circ_{1}a=\mathbf{F}^{a}
,
\mathbf{F}\circ_{2}b=\mathbf{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b$}}}
,
\mathbf{F}\circ_{3}c=\mathbf{F}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle c$}}}
and
\mathbf{F}\circ_{4}d=\mathbf{F}_{d}
. Naturality is routine. The associativity equations involving two nullary and a pseudo-binary, pseudo-ternary or pseudo-4-ary map hold as a special case of the corresponding equations for
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
.

•

In the cases of the remaining substitutions, we note that those involving unary maps are already defined — via the

. It remains to consider the higher substitutions — namely, binary into binary, ternary into binary and binary into ternary. These are defined just as in the tables — Table

and

.

\mathbf{G}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F}

Note that the substitutions of pseudo-binary and unary in the table have been defined above, so that for these to give pseudo-ternary maps, it suffices to check that the incubators in the cited appendix are invertible, which, as the composite of invertible

The remaining associativity equations then follow from the descriptions in these tables, just as for the case of
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{l}
in the preceding section. In particular, we obtain a
4
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}
and

-ary multifunctor

.

Declaring a pseudo-multimap
\mathbf{F}
to be

just when its underlying lax multimap

is tight in
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
then equips
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}
with the structure of a
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}
such that
\mathbb{U}\colon\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}\to\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
is a multifunctor of
4
-ary skew multicategories.

Theorem 6.2
.

The
4
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}
is left representable and closed, with internal hom
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
.

Proof.

We will first establish closedness. To this end, observe that evaluating the natural bijection
\lambda_{2}^{p}
in Equation
16
at
1\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\to\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
yields a pseudo binary map
\mathbf{ev}\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
such that
\lambda^{p}_{2}=\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}-
. Moreover, chasing the identity around the commutative square of Equation
16
we see that
\mathbb{U}\mathbf{(}\mathbf{ev})=ev\circ_{1}U_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
where
ev\colon\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
is the universal lax binary map of Theorem
5.2
.
This equation, plus commutativity of Equation
16
, ensure that both functions

\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}-,\lambda^{p}_{n+1}\colon\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\,\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\,)\rightrightarrows\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n+1}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B};\mathcal{C})

coincide upon post-composition by
\mathbb{U}_{n+1}
.
Our task is to prove that they coincide in general. The case
n=0
is trivial since
\mathbb{U}_{1}
is the identity function whilst the case
n=1
is true by definition of
\mathbf{ev}
. It remains to consider the cases
n=2,3
.

Consider then
\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2};\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))
. By the above, we know that
\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F}
and
\lambda^{p}_{3}\mathbf{F}
have the same underlying lax ternary maps. Therefore it remains to show that their associated pseudo-binary maps coincide. To prove this, we use that, much as in the lax case of Proposition
4.6
, the ternary map
\lambda^{p}_{3}\mathbf{F}
has components
\lambda^{p}_{2}(\mathbf{F}^{a_{1}}),\lambda^{p}_{2}(\mathbf{F}_{a_{2}})
and
\mathbf{ev}_{b}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F}
where
\mathbf{ev}_{b}\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}
denotes the evaluation Gray-functor.

We then have the first equality in the sequence

(\lambda^{p}_{3}\mathbf{F})^{a_{1}}=\lambda^{p}_{2}(\mathbf{F}^{a_{1}})=\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}(\mathbf{F}\circ_{1}a_{1})=(\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F})\circ_{1}a_{1}=(\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F})^{a_{1}}.

The second equality holds by definition of
\mathbf{ev}
, the third by associativity and the fourth by definition of substitution of nullary maps. Similarly
(\lambda^{p}_{3}\mathbf{F})\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle a_{2}$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle a_{2}$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a_{2}$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a_{2}$}}}=(\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F})\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle a_{2}$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle a_{2}$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a_{2}$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a_{2}$}}}
. Finally, we have
(\lambda^{p}_{3}\mathbf{F})_{b}=\mathbf{ev}_{b}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F}=(\mathbf{ev}\circ_{2}b)\circ_{1}\mathbf{F}=(\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F})\circ_{3}b=(\mathbf{ev}\circ_{1}\mathbf{F})_{b}
. This completes the case
n=3
and the case
n=4
is similar.

Having established that
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}
is a closed
4
-ary multicategory, we must also show that the bijections
\lambda^{p}_{n+1}
restrict to bijections on tight multimaps. So consider
\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))
. By definition it is tight just when
\mathbb{U}_{n}\mathbf{F}
is tight. But since the strict map
U_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\to\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
reflects identity 2-cells, this is the case precisely when
U_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\circ\mathbb{U}_{n}\mathbf{F}\colon\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{l}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n};\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}))
is tight. Since
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
is, by Theorem
5.2
, closed in the skew sense, this will in turn be the case just when
\lambda^{l}_{n+1}(U_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}\circ\mathbb{U}_{n}\mathbf{F})
is tight. By Equation
16
, this equals
\mathbb{U}_{n+1}(\lambda^{p}_{n+1}\mathbf{F})
, and so will be tight just when
\lambda^{p}_{n+1}\mathbf{F}
is, as required.

Having established closedness, we turn to left representability. The nullary map classifier
u\colon(-)\to\mathbf{1}
is as for
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
. Therefore, as in that setting, it remains to prove that the internal hom functor, now
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
, has a left adjoint. Arguing as in the proof of Proposition
5.6
, it suffices to show that
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},-)_{i}\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{Set}
preserves limits and is accessible for
i=0,1,2,3
. Since
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},-)_{0}=\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},-)_{0}\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(QA,-)
, the case
i=0
is as before. For
i=1
, we write
P_{+}:=\mathbf{Psd}(\mathbf{2},-)\colon\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
for the
pseudo
path space functor. It is straightforward to show that we have a bijection
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{1}\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}_{p}(\mathcal{A},P_{+}\mathcal{B})
natural in
\mathcal{B}
— equally, a natural bijection
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{1}\cong\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}(Q\mathcal{A},P_{+}\mathcal{B})
so that, again arguing as in the lax case, it suffices to prove that
P_{+}
preserves limits and is accessible. As for
P
, this is the case since
P_{+}
is representable in each component.

It remains to prove that
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},-)_{i}
preserves limits and is accessible for
i=2,3
. To this end, consider the diagram below left.

\textstyle{\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

Here

sends a modification
\theta
to the
\mathcal{A}_{1}
-indexed family of

-cells
(\theta_{f})_{f\in\mathcal{A}_{1}}
. We denote by

the inclusion of the set of invertible

-cells in
\mathcal{B}
and note that the functor

is represented by the free invertible

-cell. Since a pseudo-modification
\Lambda\colon\alpha\to\beta
is an ordinary modification for which each
\Lambda_{f}
is invertible, and for which
\alpha
and

are pseudo-transformations, the diagram above left exhibits

as a wide pullback, naturally in

. The functors

and

preserve limits and are accessible since both are composite of representables. The functor

has been covered above, whilst

Finally, the simple case of

∎

6.4.
The associated skew monoidal closed structure

Given Theorem
6.2
, the construction of Section
2.6
again yields:

Theorem 6.3
.

There is a closed skew monoidal structure
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},\mathbf{1})
whose internal hom is
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
.

Let us describe the skew monoidal structure in a little more detail.

•

The unit is the terminal Gray-category
\mathbf{1}
as before.

•

The tensor product
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{p}\mathcal{B}
is the tight pseudo-binary map classifier. It can be presented by adapting the presentation of
\mathcal{A}\otimes_{l}\mathcal{B}
in Section
5.3
by adjoining further:

2
-cells
:

\bullet

at
A\colon a\to a^{\prime}
and
B\colon b\to b^{\prime}
, a
2
-cell
A^{o}_{B}\colon T_{b^{\prime}}(A)T^{a}(B)\to T^{a^{\prime}}(B)T_{b}(A)
;

3
-cells
:

\bullet

at
A\colon a\to a^{\prime}
and
B\colon b\to b^{\prime}
,
3
-cells
\epsilon_{A,B}\colon A^{o}_{B}A_{B}\to 1
and
\eta_{A,B}\colon 1\to A_{B}A^{o}_{B}
, along with
3
-cells
(\epsilon_{A,B})^{-1}
and
(\eta_{A,B})^{-1}
;

\bullet

Further
3
-cells
(T^{\alpha}_{B})^{-1}
and
(T^{A}_{\beta})^{-1}
.

Equations
:

\bullet

The triangle equations for an adjunction
A^{o}_{B}\dashv A_{B}
plus the equations that
(\epsilon_{A,B})^{-1}
and
(\eta_{A,B})^{-1}
are the intended inverses so that we have an adjoint equivalence. Furthermore the equations asserting that
(T^{\alpha}_{B})^{-1}
and
(T^{A}_{\beta})^{-1}
are the intended inverses. Finally the equations that
A^{o}_{B},\epsilon_{A,B}
and
\eta_{A,B}
are identities whenever
A
or
B
is an identity.

•

The left unit map
l_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\mathbf{1}\otimes_{p}\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
is again the counit
p_{\mathcal{A}}\colon Q\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
whilst the right unit map
r_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\otimes_{p}\mathbf{1}
is, as before, invertible. The example of Section
6.4
again shows that the associator is not invertible.

In a followup paper, we will show that
(\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},\mathbf{1})
forms a symmetric skew monoidal structure in the sense of
[
11
]
.

7.
Restricting to strict maps in
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})

The reader may have noticed that the full sub-Gray-categories
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{s}
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})_{s}
of
\mathbf{Lax}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
and
\mathbf{Psd}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
containing the strict maps form Gray-categories too. In this section, we show that these form the internal homs of closed left representable
4
-ary multicategories
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{\sharp}
and
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{\sharp}
, and so give rise to skew monoidal closed structures on
\mathbf{G}\text{-}\mathbf{Cat}
which are both left and right normal.

In fact the
4
-ary multicategories
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{\sharp}
and
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{\sharp}
are obtained in a universal way from
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
and
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}
, by applying the construction sending a
4
-ary skew multicategory to its
4
-ary multicategory of
sharp maps
, which we introduce below.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a
k
-ary skew multicategory, and let us re-emphasise that we require that the functions
\mathbb{C}^{t}_{n}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};y)\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{l}_{n}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};y)
are subset inclusions, since this condition is used in the constructions below. The notion of sharp multimap is defined inductively, as follows.

•

Each nullary map is sharp.

•

For
n>0
, a multimap
f\colon a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\to b
is sharp if it is tight and
f\circ_{i}x
is sharp for each nullary
x\colon\diamond\to a_{i}
and
1\leq i\leq n
.

Example 7.1
.

A binary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}
(that is, a lax binary map) is sharp if it is tight and, moreover, each
F^{a}
is a Gray-functor. In more elementary terms, a lax binary map
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
is sharp just when each of
F^{a}
and
F_{b}
are Gray-functors and the
3
-cells
F^{A_{2},A_{1}}_{B}
are identities.

A binary map
\mathbf{F}\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}
(that is, a pseudo binary map) is sharp in just when its underlying lax binary map is sharp.

We let
\mathbb{C}^{\sharp}
have the same objects as
\mathbb{C}^{l}
and have multimaps the sharp ones.

Proposition 7.2
.

\mathbb{C}^{\sharp}
is a
k
-ary sub-multicategory of
\mathbb{C}^{l}
.

Proof.

The unary identities are tight and so sharp. Therefore it remains to prove that
g\circ_{i}f
is sharp if
g
and
f
are. We argue by induction on the degree
n
of
g\circ_{i}f
. If
n=0
, it is trivial, since all nullary maps are sharp. Suppose then that
g\circ_{i}f
has degree
n+1
.
Firstly, we show it is tight. If
f
is of degree
0
, then
g
has degree at least
2
. Hence since
g\circ_{i}f
is sharp of degree
\geq 1
, it is tight. Otherwise both
g
and
f
have degree at least
1
and so are both tight by assumption. Hence their composite
g\circ_{i}f
is tight.

It remains to show that
(g\circ_{i}f)\circ_{j}x
is sharp for each nullary
x
. Let
f
have degree
m
. There are two cases. If
i\leq j\leq i+m
(so that
x
is substituted inside
f
) then associativity gives us
(g\circ_{i}f)\circ_{j}x=g\circ_{p}(f\circ_{q}x)
for the appropriate
p
and
q
. In particular, the right hand side is a composite of sharp multimaps of composite degree
\leq n
and so sharp by assumption. Otherwise (
x
substituted outside of
f
) associativity gives
(g\circ_{i}f)\circ_{j}x=(g\circ_{p}x)\circ_{q}f
for suitable
p
and
q
which, again, has composite degree
\leq n
and so is sharp by induction.

∎

The
k
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{C}^{\sharp}
has a universal property. To see this, consider the full inclusion
I\colon\mathbf{Mult}_{k}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{SkMult}_{k}
viewing a
k
-ary multicategory as a
k
-ary skew multicategory in which all loose morphisms of arity
>0
are tight. It restricts to a full inclusion
I\colon\mathbf{Mult}_{k}^{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{SkMult}_{k}^{0}
where, on either side, we take the
0
-fully faithful morphisms
: those
F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
for which each function
\mathbb{C}_{0}(\diamond;a)\to\mathbb{D}_{0}(\diamond;Fa)
is a bijection.

Proposition 7.3
.

The inclusion
I\colon\mathbf{Mult}_{k}^{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{SkMult}_{k}^{0}
has a right adjoint, whose value at a
k
-ary skew multicategory
\mathbb{C}
is the
k
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{C}^{\sharp}
.

Proof.

We have an identity on objects
0
-fully faithful multifunctor
I(\mathbb{C}^{\sharp})\to\mathbb{C}
which we will show the be the counit of the adjunction. This amounts to showing, given a
k
-ary multicategory
\mathbb{D}
and a multifunctor
F\colon I(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{C}
, that each multimorphism in the image of
F
is sharp and we prove this by induction. The case
n=0
is trivial since each nullary multimorphism is sharp. Suppose it is true for multimaps of degree
\leq n
, and consider
f\colon a_{1},\ldots,a_{n+1}\to b\in I(\mathbb{D})
. Since
f
is tight, so is
Ff
. Given
y\colon\diamond\to Fa_{i}\in\mathbb{C}
, it remains to show that
Ff\circ_{i}y
is sharp. But since
F
is
0
-fully faithful, there exists a unique nullary map
x\colon\diamond\to a_{i}\in I(\mathbb{D})
such that
Fx=y
. Then
Ff\circ_{i}y=Ff\circ_{i}Fx=F(f\circ_{i}x)
which is sharp by induction, since
f\circ_{i}x
has degree
n
.
∎

In order to prove that
\mathbb{L}\mathbf{ax}^{\sharp}
and
\mathbb{P}\mathbf{sd}^{\sharp}
are left representable, we will use the following result.

Proposition 7.4
.

Let
k\geq 2
. If
\mathbb{C}
is a left representable
k
-ary skew multicategory and the category of tight unary maps
\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}
is cocomplete, then
\mathbb{C}^{\sharp}
admits binary and nullary map classifiers.

Proof.

The nullary map classifier
i
is unchanged. Now a tight binary map
f\colon a,b\to c
is sharp just when for each nullary map
x\colon\diamond\to a
, the composite
f\circ_{1}x\colon b\to c
is tight. Let
\overline{f}\colon a\otimes b\to c
denote the corresponding map out of the tight binary map classifier and
\overline{x}\colon i\to a
the corresponding map out of
i
. Expressed in these terms, the condition that
f\circ_{1}x\colon b\to c
is tight says that the (upper horizontal, right vertical) composite in the diagram below factors through
l_{b}\colon i\otimes b\to c
as depicted.

\textstyle{i\otimes b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{l_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\overline{x}\otimes 1}
\textstyle{a\otimes b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{f}}
\textstyle{b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\exists}
\textstyle{c}

Here
l_{b}\colon i\otimes b\to b
is the left unit map of the corresponding skew monoidal structure. Note that
l_{b}
is epi since, following Section
2.6
, it is the counit of the adjunction
i\otimes-\dashv j
with faithful right adjoint
j\colon\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{l}_{1}
. In particular, such a factorisation is unique.

We can express the condition for all
\overline{x}
simultaneously by requiring that the (upper horizontal, right vertical) composite in the diagram below left

\textstyle{\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(i,a).i\otimes b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(i,a).l_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\epsilon}
\textstyle{a\otimes b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{f}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(i,a).b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\exists}
\textstyle{c}

\textstyle{\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(i,a).i\otimes b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(i,a).l_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\epsilon}
\textstyle{a\otimes b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbb{C}^{t}_{1}(i,a).b\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

factors through the left vertical epimorphism, where

is the morphism from the copower whose component at

is
\overline{x}\otimes 1\colon i\otimes b\to a\otimes b
. Accordingly, such an
\overline{f}
bijectively corresponds to a map out of the pushout
